title: Information System Security
text:
Stream Ciphers

Principle
Stream cipher: family of cryptosystems where the encrypted block = 1 bit.
Two phases:

Generation of the keystream \(z_i\) (depends on the key k).
Substitution: combination of the plaintext \(m_i\) with \(z_i\) (often an xor \(\oplus\)).







TipIntuition



Canonical example: the one-time pad. Generation = pure randomness, substitution = xor.




Characteristics
🔴 Advantages: speed (registers), low CPU cost, no memory/buffering, limited/absent error propagation (retransmission is enough → suited to WiFi).
🟠 Drawbacks: robustness = quality of the keystream’s randomness; reusing the keystream breaks security (cf. one-time pad).


Synchronous vs Asynchronous









Synchronous
Asynchronous (self-synchronizing)




Keystream depends on
key k alone
key k + t previous ciphertexts


Formula
\(\sigma_{i+1}=f(\sigma_i,k)\), \(z_i=g(\sigma_i,k)\), \(c_i=h(z_i,m_i)\)
\(\sigma_i=(c_{i-t},\ldots,c_{i-1})\), \(z_i=g(\sigma_i,k)\), \(c_i=h(z_i,m_i)\)


Synchronization
required (same state at sender/receiver)
self-synchronization via buffer


Error propagation
none
limited to buffer size t


Active attacks (insert./delete)
not directly detected
better detected (propagation)


Statistical diffusion of the plaintext
weak
strong → useful if plaintext entropy is limited









WarningPitfall



Synchronous = no error propagation BUT deleting a ciphertext → loss of synchronization. Asynchronous = propagation limited to the buffer, but self-recovery is possible.


Additive stream cipher (most frequent synchronous case): \(c_i = m_i \oplus z_i\), keystream produced by a pseudo-random generator driven by k.


Keystream generators
LFSR (Linear Feedback Shift Register): generates a long keystream (m bits) from a short key (l bits, \(l \ll m\)).

well suited to hardware;
long periods, good apparent randomness;
based on linear combinations.

🟠 Insufficient security on its own (especially historical military use) → measured by linear complexity, computable via the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm.
Solution: replace the linear combination with a non-linear function f → NLFSR (Non Linear Feedback Shift Register), more robust.


RC4

Created in 1987 (Ron Rivest, RSA Security), variable key, 10× faster than DES.
Synchronous mode: keystream independent of the plaintext/ciphertext.
Core: S-box 8×8 = permutation of values 0–255, a function of the key with \(0 < len(k) \le 255\).
Final encryption: \(c_i = m_i \oplus z_i\) (xor with keystream).
Two steps:








Step
Role




KSA (Key Scheduling Algorithm)
fills the S-box based on the key


PRGA (Pseudo Random Generator Algorithm)
generates the keystream from the S-box









WarningPitfall



RC4 is broken in practice: major flaws in the key scheduling and the PRGA, exploited notably against the WiFi WEP protocol.

title: Information System Security
text:
Block Ciphers

Definition
A block cipher = a bijective function \(\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^n\) parameterized by a k-bit key (n = nominal size). Each key ↔︎ a different bijection.


Quality criteria







Criterion
Requirement




Key entropy
equiprobable, ≥ 128 bits (brute-force resistance)


Performance
execution speed


Block size
≥ 128 bits (avoids dictionary attacks)


Cryptanalytic resistance
robust against linear/differential/meet-in-the-middle attacks, effort ≈ brute force





Modes of operation










Mode
Identical plaintexts →
Error propagation
Parallelizable
Distinctive feature




ECB
identical ciphertexts
none (independent blocks)
yes
weak (visible patterns)


CBC
different ciphertexts (if IV changes)
error in \(c_j\) affects \(c_j\) and \(c_{j+1}\)
no (chaining)
erases plaintext patterns


CFB
different (if IV changes)
error in the next \(n/r\) ciphertexts
no
behaves like an asynchronous stream cipher (keystream depends on previous ciphertexts)


OFB
different (if IV changes)
none
no (sequential keystream)
behaves like a synchronous stream cipher (keystream = f(key, IV) alone)


CTR
different (counter changes)
none
yes (random access)
keystream = encryption of an incremented counter; never reuse a counter









WarningPitfall



Do not confuse CFB (asynchronous, depends on the ciphertexts) with OFB (synchronous, depends only on the key + IV). For OFB and CTR: change the IV/counter if the key stays the same, or you risk reusing the keystream.




Product Ciphers & Feistel Ciphers
Product cipher: successive combination of transpositions, substitutions, xors, etc.
Feistel cipher: an iterative product cipher. A \(2t\)-bit plaintext \((L_0,R_0)\) → ciphertext \((R_r,L_r)\) after r stages.
\[
L_i = R_{i-1} \qquad R_i = L_{i-1} \oplus f(R_{i-1}, K_i)
\]

each stage is a bijection (invertible);
subkeys \(K_i\) derived from K, different at each stage;
r even, \(\ge 3\) (DES: 16 stages);
decryption = the same process, subkeys in reverse order (\(K_r \to K_1\)).



DES (Data Encryption Standard)



Property
Value




Type
Feistel cipher


Block size
64 bits


Effective key size
56 bits (64 bits with parity)


Stages
16, 48-bit subkeys


Compatible modes
ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB



Internal function (per stage): Expansion E (32→48 bits) → xor with subkey → 8 S-boxes (48→32 bits) → permutation P. Framed by the initial/final permutations IP/IP⁻¹ over the 64 bits.



DES operating scheme








WarningPitfall



DES is not a group under composition: \(E_{K_2}(E_{K_1}(x)) \ne E_{K_3}(x)\) in general. This is what justifies Triple DES actually increasing security (otherwise exhaustive search would suffice regardless of the number of executions).


Weak keys: \(K\) is weak if \(E_K(E_K(x))=x\); a pair is semi-weak if \(E_{K_1}(E_{K_2}(x))=x\). DES: 4 weak keys, 6 semi-weak pairs (subkeys repeated in pairs → cryptanalysis made easier).
Triple DES (3DES): Encryption-Decryption-Encryption with 2 or 3 keys → key space \(\{0,1\}^{112}\). Breaks DES’s brute-force limit (24h in 1999 with 100,000 PCs), but at a cost = 3× the computation time of DES.



Triple-DES: Encryption / Decryption / Encryption




AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)



Property
Value




Adopted
2001 (Daemen & Rijmen, formerly Rijndael)


Type
iterative block cipher, not a Feistel cipher


Block size
128 bits


Key size
128 / 192 / 256 bits


Stages
10 (128 bits) / +1 per +32 bits of key (14 for 256 bits)


Algebraic field
\(GF(2^8)\) (polynomials of degree ≤7 over \(GF(2)\))



4 operations per stage (on a 4×4 matrix of bytes):







Operation
Role




ByteSub
non-linear substitution (S-box), resists linear/differential cryptanalysis


ShiftRow
permutation, row shifting


MixColumn
linear combination of the columns (matrix multiplication)


AddRoundKey
xor with the stage’s subkey






Detail of an AES stage (round)


Decryption: inverse operations (InvSubBytes, InvShiftRows, InvMixColumns); AddRoundKey is its own inverse (xor).
Key Schedule: expansion of the main key into a \(4 \times 4(N_e+1)\) matrix, then split into subkeys (4 columns each).






TipIntuition



AES ≈ 2× faster than DES in software and theoretically ~\(10^{22}\) times more secure.


Known attacks (none practical):

XSL (Courtois-Pieprzyk): AES ↔︎ a system of 8000 quadratic equations, 1600 unknowns, estimated effort \(2^{100}\).
Related-key attacks: results on reduced versions of AES.
Biclique meet-in-the-middle (2015): reduces the AES-128 effort to \(2^{126}\) (factor of 4 vs. brute force) — still out of reach.
Side-channel attacks (cache-timing): key extraction via the implementation (6-7 plaintext/ciphertext pairs are enough in some cases).
Security always depends on a maximum-entropy key (weak passwords = a real practical weakness, e.g. WPA2).



Cryptanalysis of block ciphers









Technique
Attack type
Principle
Cost (on DES)




Differential
chosen plaintext
propagation of differences between 2 plaintexts through the stages
\(2^{47}\) chosen plaintext pairs


Linear
known plaintext
linear approximations of the block cipher, probabilistic analysis
\(2^{38}\) (10% success) to \(2^{43}\) (85%) known plaintexts


Meet-in-the-middle
known plaintext
applies to \(y=E_{K_2}(E_{K_1}(x))\): builds 2 lists (\(2^{56}\) elements) and looks for collisions
\(2^{57}\) operations + \(2^{56}\) storage (≪ naive \(2^{112}\))









WarningPitfall



The effectiveness of linear/differential attacks increases exponentially as the number of stages decreases — hence the cryptographic value of having a large number of rounds.

title: Information System Security
text:
Key takeaways

Stream cipher = 1 bit at a time, keystream generation + xor; synchronous (key alone) vs. asynchronous (+ previous ciphertexts, self-synchronization, propagation limited to the buffer).
LFSR/NLFSR generate the keystream from a short key; RC4 = KSA (S-box init) + PRGA (generation), broken in practice (WEP).
Block cipher = a bijective function per block; quality = key entropy + block size + cryptanalytic resistance.
Modes: ECB (no chaining, weak), CBC (chaining, error limited to 2 blocks), CFB (asynchronous), OFB (synchronous), CTR (parallelizable, no error propagation).
Feistel cipher: \(L_i=R_{i-1}\), \(R_i=L_{i-1}\oplus f(R_{i-1},K_i)\) — DES is an example (16 stages, 56-bit key); DES is not a group → this justifies 3DES.
AES: not a Feistel cipher, 128-bit blocks, \(GF(2^8)\), 4 operations per stage (ByteSub, ShiftRow, MixColumn, AddRoundKey), 10 to 14 stages depending on the key.
Cryptanalysis: differential (chosen plaintext), linear (known plaintext, the most powerful in practice), meet-in-the-middle (attacks compositions \(E_{K_2}(E_{K_1}(x))\)).

title: Information System Security
text:
### What fundamentally defines a stream cipher as opposed to a block cipher?

> Compare the size of the unit that is actually encrypted in each family.

1. [ ] A stream cipher always uses a shorter key than a block cipher
1. [x] A stream cipher encrypts bit by bit, whereas a block cipher encrypts blocks of n bits
    > Correct: the fundamental structural difference is the size of the encrypted unit (1 bit vs. a block).
1. [ ] A stream cipher is always asymmetric
    > Incorrect: both families are symmetric (same key to encrypt/decrypt).
1. [ ] A stream cipher cannot use an xor operation
    > Incorrect: on the contrary, xor is the most common substitution operation in stream ciphers.


### Which statements correctly describe stream ciphers?

> Think back to both the advantages AND the drawbacks presented in the course.

- [x] They require little or no memory/buffering
    > Correct: this is a central characteristic, linked to bit-by-bit processing.
- [x] Reusing the keystream seriously compromises security
    > Correct: this is the classic weakness illustrated by the one-time pad.
- [ ] They are slower than a block cipher because they require more computation per bit
    > Incorrect: on the contrary, they are known to be very fast, well suited to "on the fly" encryption.
- [ ] Their robustness does not depend on the quality of the random generator used
    > Incorrect: robustness in fact depends heavily on the quality (randomness) of the generated keystream.


### A stream cipher necessarily needs more CPU resources than a block cipher to encrypt the same amount of data.

> Think back to one of the arguments in favor of stream ciphers given in the course.

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: one of the advantages highlighted is precisely their low CPU cost, well suited to resource-limited systems.


### A video streaming application needs to encrypt a continuous, real-time data stream, with packets sometimes lost during transmission. Why is a stream cipher (rather than a classic block cipher in a chained mode) often well suited to this context?

> Think about error propagation and how packet loss is handled.

1. [ ] Because a stream cipher can never be broken by cryptanalysis
    > Incorrect: no system presented is described as unbreakable; RC4, for example, has been broken.
1. [x] Because error propagation is limited or absent, which tolerates packet loss well
    > Correct: the course explicitly states that this property makes stream ciphers well suited to transmissions with frequent losses (WiFi, streaming).
1. [ ] Because a stream cipher never requires a secret key
    > Incorrect: a stream cipher does use a secret key k, like any symmetric system.
1. [ ] Because block encryption is always slower in every context
    > Incorrect: the course does not make this general claim; error propagation is the key argument here.


### In a synchronous stream cipher, what does the keystream generated at step i depend on?

> Look carefully at the arguments of the functions f and g in the course's equations.

1. [ ] On the plaintext m_i only
1. [ ] On the ciphertext c_i only
1. [x] On the internal state and the key k, but not on the plaintext or the ciphertext
    > Correct: this is precisely what distinguishes synchronous mode from asynchronous mode.
1. [ ] On the previous t ciphertexts only
    > Incorrect: this dependency characterizes asynchronous mode, not synchronous mode.


### A sender and a receiver using an asynchronous (self-synchronizing) stream cipher temporarily lose synchronization following the deletion of a ciphertext in transit. What happens next, according to the course?

> Think about the role of the buffer of previous ciphertexts in generating the asynchronous keystream.

1. [ ] The receiver remains permanently out of sync, as in the synchronous case
    > Incorrect: it is in fact the opposite; self-synchronization is the distinctive property of asynchronous mode.
1. [x] The receiver automatically regains synchronization after a number of ciphertexts equal to the buffer size
    > Correct: the asynchronous keystream depends on the last t ciphertexts; once this buffer has been refreshed with correct ciphertexts, synchronization is restored.
1. [ ] The entire communication must be restarted from scratch with a new key
    > Incorrect: no complete restart is necessary; self-synchronization happens automatically.
1. [ ] The loss of synchronization has no observable effect on decryption
    > Incorrect: it causes error propagation limited to the buffer size, so it is not without effect.


### An engineer needs to encrypt highly redundant plaintexts (for example, near-identical protocol headers), with a risk of targeted statistical attacks. Which type of stream cipher does the course recommend favoring in this case, and why?

> The course explicitly links one type of stream cipher to better diffusion of the plaintext's statistics.

1. [ ] Synchronous, because it propagates no errors
1. [x] Asynchronous, because each plaintext bit influences all subsequent ciphertexts, which better disperses the statistics
    > Correct: the course explicitly recommends asynchronous stream ciphers when plaintext entropy is limited.
1. [ ] Synchronous, because it requires less buffer memory
    > Incorrect: the question is about protection against redundant statistics, not about memory.
1. [ ] Neither of the two; a block cipher must be used in this case
    > Incorrect: the course states a preference between the two types of stream ciphers, not a rejection of stream ciphers.


### Which of the following are correct characteristics of an LFSR (Linear Feedback Shift Register), according to the course?

> Think back to both the practical advantages and the security limitations of LFSRs.

- [x] It adapts very well to hardware implementations
    > Correct: this is one of the highlighted advantages.
- [x] It produces long-period sequences with notable randomness
    > Correct: this is explicitly mentioned as a property of the LFSR.
- [ ] It nowadays offers a level of security comparable to modern block ciphers
    > Incorrect: the course states that the security of LFSR-based systems is considered insufficient compared to block ciphers.
- [ ] Its linear complexity cannot be computed algorithmically
    > Incorrect: the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm makes it possible to compute exactly this linear complexity.


### Why were NLFSRs (Non Linear Feedback Shift Registers) introduced to replace classic LFSRs?

> Think about the main weakness of LFSRs mentioned in the course, related to their algebraic nature.

1. [ ] To reduce the required key length
1. [x] To increase the (linear) complexity, and thus resistance to cryptanalysis, by replacing the linear combination with a non-linear function f
    > Correct: the course explicitly presents NLFSRs as a solution to increase complexity in response to the weakness of purely linear combinations.
1. [ ] To allow the use of variable-length keys, which LFSRs do not allow
1. [ ] Because LFSRs cannot be implemented in hardware
    > Incorrect: it is the opposite; LFSRs are known to be well suited to hardware.


### RC4: which of these statements correctly describes the algorithm, according to the course?

> Think back to how RC4 operates and its history.

1. [ ] RC4 is an asynchronous stream cipher whose keystream depends on the previous ciphertexts
    > Incorrect: RC4 operates in synchronous mode, independent of the ciphertext and the plaintext.
1. [x] RC4 relies on a 256-value S-box, built from a variable-length key
    > Correct: the 8x8 S-box (a permutation of 0 to 255) is the key element of RC4, initialized based on the key.
1. [ ] RC4 has remained entirely confidential and has never been the subject of public analysis
    > Incorrect: after it leaked in 1994, it was widely studied by the cryptographic community.
1. [ ] RC4 is slower than DES in a software implementation
    > Incorrect: the course states that RC4 is about 10 times faster than DES.


### What is the difference in role between the KSA and the PRGA in RC4?

> Think about what result each of these two algorithms produces.

1. [ ] The KSA generates the final keystream, the PRGA initializes the S-box
1. [x] The KSA initializes and scrambles the S-box based on the key; the PRGA then generates the keystream from this S-box
    > Correct: this is exactly the division of roles described in the course (Key Scheduling, then Pseudo Random Generation).
1. [ ] The KSA and the PRGA perform exactly the same operation, one after the other
1. [ ] The PRGA is executed before the KSA in the algorithm's flow
    > Incorrect: the S-box must first be built by the KSA before the PRGA can generate the keystream.


### Put the steps of how RC4 works in chronological order.

> Think about what must exist before a keystream can be generated.

1. Initialization of S as the identity permutation (0, 1, ..., N-1)
2. Scrambling of S based on the key K (KSA loop)
3. Iterative generation of the keystream via the PRGA loop
4. Final encryption of the plaintext by xor with the generated keystream


### The use of RC4 in the WiFi WEP protocol was considered secure for many years and was never compromised in practice.

> Think back to what the course says about RC4 applied to WEP.

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: the course explicitly states that the application of RC4 to WEP was "broken" following a flaw in the way the protocol was used.


### What property MUST the function associated with a block cipher have, to allow unique decryption?

> Think about what guarantees that a given ciphertext corresponds to only one possible plaintext.

1. [ ] It must be linear
1. [ ] It must commute with the key-generation function
1. [x] It must be bijective
    > Correct: each key defines a different bijection, a necessary condition for unique decryption to be possible.
1. [ ] It must produce an output block larger than the input block
    > Incorrect: a block cipher maps an n-bit block to another block of the same size n.


### Which criteria can be used to evaluate the quality of a modern block cipher, according to the course?

> Think back to the four criteria presented (key, performance, block size, resistance).

- [x] High key entropy, with keys of at least 128 bits
    > Correct: this is an explicit criterion for resisting brute-force attacks.
- [x] A sufficiently large block size (typically at least 128 bits)
    > Correct: a block that is too small would allow plaintext/ciphertext dictionary attacks.
- [ ] The mandatory use of a Feistel-type structure
    > Incorrect: AES, for example, is a modern block cipher that is not a Feistel cipher.
- [ ] The total absence of any non-linear operation
    > Incorrect: non-linear operations (S-boxes) are, on the contrary, essential to cryptographic resistance.


### An attacker observes that two identical plaintext blocks systematically produce two identical ciphertext blocks in a system encrypted with a block cipher. Which mode of operation is most likely being used?

> Think about the mode that involves no chaining between blocks.

1. [ ] CBC
    > Incorrect: in CBC, identical plaintexts produce different ciphertexts thanks to chaining (if the IV changes).
1. [x] ECB
    > Correct: the lack of chaining in ECB means that identical plaintexts always produce the same ciphertexts, which is precisely its well-known weakness.
1. [ ] CTR
    > Incorrect: in CTR, the counter changes for each block, so identical plaintexts produce different ciphertexts.
1. [ ] OFB
    > Incorrect: in OFB, if the IV changes, identical plaintexts also produce different ciphertexts.


### An application needs to encrypt and transmit very large volumes of data at high speed, with a need for random access to individual blocks and heavy parallelization of computations. Which mode of operation is the best fit?

> Think about the mode for which the course explicitly highlights the absence of dependency between blocks and SIMD compatibility.

1. [ ] CBC, because it provides the best chaining between blocks
1. [ ] CFB, because it behaves like a stream cipher
1. [x] CTR, because it allows random access to the blocks and full parallelization, with no dependency between them
    > Correct: the course explicitly states that counter mode fully takes advantage of SIMD architectures and allows random access to each block.
1. [ ] ECB, because each block is processed independently of the others
    > Incorrect: although ECB is parallelizable, it provides no protection against identifying identical blocks, unlike CTR, which remains secure on this point.


### What is the fundamental difference in operation between the CFB and OFB modes, both derived from a block cipher?

> Think back to the synchronous or asynchronous nature of each of these two modes.

1. [ ] CFB is synchronous (keystream depends only on the key and the IV), whereas OFB is asynchronous (keystream depends on the previous ciphertexts)
    > Incorrect: it is the opposite: CFB depends on the previous ciphertexts (asynchronous), OFB depends only on the key and the IV (synchronous).
1. [x] CFB is asynchronous (the keystream depends on the previous ciphertexts), whereas OFB is synchronous (the keystream depends only on the key and the IV)
    > Correct: this is exactly the distinction given in the course between these two modes.
1. [ ] Both modes are strictly synchronous and work identically
1. [ ] Both modes are strictly asynchronous and work identically
    > Incorrect: the two modes behave differently with respect to their dependency on the ciphertext.


### In a Feistel-type cipher, we have a plaintext (L0, R0) and a stage function f with subkeys K_i. After a stage i, how is R_i computed?

> Apply directly the formula for a Feistel stage presented in the course.

1. [ ] R_i = R_{i-1} XOR f(L_{i-1}, K_i)
1. [x] R_i = L_{i-1} XOR f(R_{i-1}, K_i)
    > Correct: this is exactly the course's formula, with L_i = R_{i-1} and R_i = L_{i-1} XOR f(R_{i-1}, K_i).
1. [ ] R_i = L_{i-1} AND f(R_{i-1}, K_i)
1. [ ] R_i = f(L_{i-1}, R_{i-1})
    > Incorrect: the subkey K_i explicitly appears in the formula, and the combining operation is an xor, not a simple application of f without combination.


### Which statements about DES are correct, according to the course?

> Think back to the structure, block size, key size, and number of stages of DES.

- [x] DES is a Feistel cipher with 16 stages
    > Correct: this is exactly the structure described in the course.
- [x] The effective size of the DES key is 56 usable bits (out of 64 transmitted bits, with parity bits)
    > Correct: this is explicitly stated in the course.
- [ ] DES uses 128-bit blocks, like AES
    > Incorrect: DES uses 64-bit blocks, unlike AES, which uses 128 bits.
- [ ] DES forms an algebraic group under the composition operation
    > Incorrect: the course explicitly states that DES is not a group under composition.


### Why is the fact that "DES is not a group" (under composition) a cryptographically important property?

> Think about what this property guarantees regarding Triple DES.

1. [ ] Because it makes DES completely unbreakable by brute force
1. [x] Because it guarantees that successively applying DES with different keys (as in Triple DES) actually increases security, instead of being equivalent to a single DES with another key
    > Correct: if DES were a group, one could always find a key K3 equivalent to two successive applications, which would make Triple DES useless against an exhaustive 56-bit search.
1. [ ] Because it makes it possible to reduce the required block size
1. [ ] Because it prevents the existence of weak keys
    > Incorrect: DES nevertheless has weak and semi-weak keys, a property independent of the group question.


### What characterizes a so-called "weak" key K for DES?

> Think back to the mathematical condition given in the course for a weak key.

1. [ ] E_K(x) always produces the same ciphertext regardless of x
1. [x] Applying the encryption twice with K gives back the original plaintext: E_K(E_K(x)) = x
    > Correct: this is exactly the definition given in the course, linked to the generation of subkeys that are identical in pairs.
1. [ ] K contains only bits set to 1
1. [ ] K can only be used in ECB mode
    > Incorrect: nothing in the course restricts weak keys to a particular mode of operation.


### A system uses Triple DES with an effective key space of 112 bits. What is the main practical drawback of this solution compared to plain DES, according to the course?

> Think about the performance cost of repeatedly executing the algorithm.

1. [ ] Triple DES requires a 256-bit block, incompatible with existing hardware
1. [x] Running three successive passes of DES hurts performance, which remains a drawback for certain applications
    > Correct: the course explicitly identifies this performance impact as a drawback of the solution.
1. [ ] Triple DES cannot be used with existing DES hardware or software
    > Incorrect: on the contrary, the course points out that this solution makes it possible to keep using existing DES "boxes".
1. [ ] Triple DES is actually less secure than plain DES
    > Incorrect: the course states, on the contrary, that the level of security obtained is very satisfactory.


### What structural differences distinguish AES from DES, according to the course?

> Think back to the overall structure (Feistel or not), the block size, and the algebraic field used.

- [x] AES is not a Feistel cipher, unlike DES
    > Correct: the course explicitly specifies that AES is an iterative block cipher, but not a Feistel cipher.
- [x] AES operates on 128-bit blocks, whereas DES operates on 64-bit blocks
    > Correct: this is an explicit difference in nominal size between the two algorithms.
- [ ] AES was designed secretly, without public consultation, unlike DES
    > Incorrect: it is the opposite: AES resulted from a consultation process open to experts worldwide, unlike the more closed development of DES.
- [ ] AES systematically uses 16 stages, like DES
    > Incorrect: the number of AES stages varies depending on the key size (10, 12, or 14 stages); it is not fixed at 16.


### A system uses AES with a 256-bit key. How many stages (rounds) does this cipher perform, given that a 128-bit key requires 10 stages and each 32-bit increase adds one stage?

> Compute the number of 32-bit increments between 128 and 256 bits, then add this number to 10.

1. [ ] 10 stages
1. [ ] 12 stages
1. [x] 14 stages
    > Correct: (256-128)/32 = 4 additional stages, i.e. 10 + 4 = 14 stages, which matches exactly the value given in the course for a 256-bit key.
1. [ ] 16 stages
    > Incorrect: this number corresponds to the number of DES stages, not the number of AES stages for a 256-bit key.


### Put the four operations performed at each AES stage (round) in order.

> Think about the order in which substitution, shifting, column mixing, and subkey addition typically occur within a stage.

1. ByteSub (non-linear substitution via S-box)
2. ShiftRow (row shifting)
3. MixColumn (linear combination of the columns)
4. AddRoundKey (xor with the stage's subkey)


### What is the specific role of the MixColumn operation in an AES stage?

> Think back to what this operation does to the columns of the state matrix.

1. [ ] It applies a non-linear substitution to each byte independently
    > Incorrect: this description corresponds to ByteSub, not MixColumn.
1. [x] It replaces each column with a linear combination of the other columns, via a matrix multiplication
    > Correct: this is exactly the description given in the course for MixColumn.
1. [ ] It performs an xor between the current state matrix and the stage's subkey
    > Incorrect: this operation is AddRoundKey, not MixColumn.
1. [ ] It shifts the rows of the matrix by a variable number of positions
    > Incorrect: this operation is ShiftRow, not MixColumn.


### What fundamental difference distinguishes differential cryptanalysis from linear cryptanalysis?

> Think about the type of plaintexts each attack requires (imposed by the attacker or merely observed).

1. [ ] Differential cryptanalysis is a known plaintext attack, linear cryptanalysis is a chosen plaintext attack
    > Incorrect: it is the opposite according to the course.
1. [x] Differential cryptanalysis is a chosen plaintext attack that studies the propagation of differences, whereas linear cryptanalysis is a known plaintext attack based on linear approximations
    > Correct: this is exactly the distinction given in the course.
1. [ ] Both techniques require physical access to the hardware executing the encryption
    > Incorrect: this description corresponds more to side-channel attacks, not to differential or linear cryptanalysis.
1. [ ] Both techniques are purely theoretical and have never been used to attack DES
    > Incorrect: the course gives concrete estimates of the number of plaintext pairs needed to attack DES with these two techniques.


### A meet-in-the-middle attack targets a scheme of the form y = E_{K2}(E_{K1}(x)), with a combined key space of 112 bits. Why is this attack markedly more efficient than a naive exhaustive search over the 2^112 possible combinations?

> Think about how two intermediate lists make it possible to recover the keys without exploring every combination.

1. [ ] Because it directly guesses the final key without any intermediate computation
1. [x] Because it builds two lists of 2^56 elements each (one per partial encryption) and looks for collisions between them, bringing the effort down to about 2^57 operations rather than 2^112
    > Correct: this is exactly the principle described in the course, with an effort and storage requirement far lower than the intuitive estimate of 2^112.
1. [ ] Because it requires no known plaintext, unlike other attacks
    > Incorrect: the attack does require known plaintexts to verify the hypothesis about candidate keys.
1. [ ] Because it exploits a weakness specific to DES's weak keys
    > Incorrect: the meet-in-the-middle principle applies generally to double-encryption-type constructions, independently of weak keys.


### How does the effectiveness of differential and linear attacks change as the number of stages (rounds) of a block cipher decreases?

> Think back to the relationship described between the number of stages and the chances of success of these attacks.

1. [ ] It decreases, because fewer stages leave less time to accumulate statistical data
1. [x] It increases exponentially, which explains why a sufficient number of stages is essential to a block cipher's security
    > Correct: the course explicitly states that the chances of success of these attacks increase exponentially as the number of stages decreases.
1. [ ] It remains strictly constant, regardless of the number of stages
1. [ ] It drops to zero below a certain number of stages
    > Incorrect: the course does not mention a cutoff threshold, but a continuous exponential trend.

title: Information System Security
text:
### Which TTP mode does a Key Distribution Center (KDC) operate under?

> The KDC participates in real time, but do A and B communicate directly with each other?

1. [ ] In-line
1. [x] On-line
    > Correct: the KDC intervenes in real time (session key generation, tickets) but A and B then communicate directly.
1. [ ] Off-line
    > Incorrect: off-line corresponds to CAs, which do not participate in the exchange in real time.


### Which statements correctly describe the off-line mode?

> Compare what a system gains and loses in off-line mode compared to the in-line/on-line modes.

- [x] The TTP does not need to be available at all times.
    > Correct: the information (the certificates) is made available a priori, without real-time intervention.
- [ ] Exchanges between A and B require the TTP for every transaction.
    > Incorrect: this is characteristic of in-line, not off-line.
- [x] Revocation of privileges is more complex to manage.
    > Correct: a key compromise is only detected asynchronously (via CRL), unlike in the real-time modes.
- [ ] It is the mode used by Key Distribution Centers.
    > Incorrect: KDCs operate in on-line mode (possibly in-line), not off-line.


### Why do Certification Authorities publish CRLs even though they operate in off-line mode?

> Think about what can invalidate a certificate after it has been signed and distributed.

1. [ ] Because the CA must periodically confirm each certificate for it to remain valid.
    > Incorrect: this rather describes the short-validity certificate strategy, an alternative solution.
1. [x] Because the theft of a private key can invalidate an already distributed certificate, asynchronously.
    > Correct: cached certificates can circulate freely; the CRL makes it possible to flag, after the fact, certificates that have become invalid.
1. [ ] Because off-line mode forbids caching certificates.
    > Incorrect: on the contrary, certificates can be cached anywhere since they are signed.


### An organization wants to minimize the availability constraints on its trust infrastructure, even if it means accepting heavier revocation management. Which TTP mode is most consistent with this objective?

> Which mode does not require the TTP to be constantly reachable?

1. [ ] In-line
1. [ ] On-line
1. [x] Off-line
    > Correct: this is exactly the trade-off of the off-line mode (typically CAs): low availability required, more complex revocation.


### Without a KDC, a symmetric system of 100 entities requires approximately how many different keys for each pair to share a unique key?

> Use the formula n(n-1)/2 with n = 100.

1. [ ] 100
1. [ ] 200
1. [x] About 4950
    > Correct: n(n-1)/2 = 100 x 99 / 2 = 4950, i.e. on the order of n².
1. [ ] About 10000


### With a KDC in place, how many new keys must be generated when a new entity joins a system of 100 entities?

> Compare with the case without a KDC, where adding an entity generated n new keys.

1. [x] Just 1 key (shared with the KDC)
    > Correct: this is precisely the benefit of the KDC's scalability: a single key per new entity instead of n.
1. [ ] 100 new keys
1. [ ] 4950 new keys


### Which problems are specifically associated with KDCs (and not directly with CAs)?

> Think about the usual operating mode of a KDC and what this implies in terms of availability and performance.

- [x] Single point of operational failure (the system is paralyzed if the KDC is unavailable).
    > Correct: the KDC's on-line mode makes the system dependent on its real-time availability.
- [x] Performance bottleneck linked to repeated cryptographic operations.
    > Correct: every exchange calls on the KDC (encryption, random generation), which can create a bottleneck.
- [ ] The need to publish revocation lists.
    > Incorrect: CRLs are specific to CAs, not KDCs.
- [ ] Impossibility of caching the distributed information.
    > Incorrect: this constraint does not specifically apply to the KDC; moreover it is not an issue identified in the course for KDCs.


### A CA has its private signing key compromised. Which statement best describes the severity of this situation compared to the compromise of a KDC?

> The course describes this consequence as "less obvious but almost as harmful."

1. [ ] The compromise of a CA is completely harmless, unlike that of a KDC.
1. [x] It has consequences that are less immediately visible than the compromise of a KDC, but almost as serious.
    > Correct: unlike the KDC (immediate and total impact), the impact of a compromised CA is mainly felt through fraudulent certificates issued, which are less visible at first glance.
1. [ ] It is strictly more serious because it also affects the system's availability.
    > Incorrect: availability is not the main issue here; it is the authenticity of the identity-key associations that is compromised.


### Why is simply verifying A's identity not enough to create a certificate associating A with its public key?

> What happens if someone else knows A's public key but not its private key?

1. [ ] Because A's identity changes too often.
1. [x] Because it is also necessary to prove that A truly possesses the corresponding private key (Proof of Possession).
    > Correct: without PoP, an attacker can have a public key that is not their own certified, based on a document already signed by the true owner.
1. [ ] Because the CA cannot generate a certificate without a digital passport.


### Put the steps of the attack described in the course against a CA that does not verify Proof of Possession back in order.

> Think about who sends what, and who intercepts the initial message.

1. C, the attacker, obtains from its own CA a certificate linking its identity to the same public key used by A.
2. A signs a document describing an invention and sends it to B along with its certificate signed by its CA.
3. C intercepts the packet sent by A to B.
4. C sends B the document signed by A, together with its own fraudulent certificate.


### In the Proof of Possession verification protocol, what is the purpose of the random value r sent by the CA to A?

> Think about what prevents an attacker from having a message of their choosing signed in advance.

1. [ ] To encrypt A's public key.
1. [x] To protect A against chosen message attacks, by ensuring that the signature covers an unpredictable value.
    > Correct: r is a random number; A signs (A, r), which prevents an attacker from preparing a valid signature in advance.
1. [ ] To indicate the validity period of the future certificate.


### An adversary possesses the private key used both to sign certificates and CRLs for a CA. What can it do against a victim A under the authority of that CA?

> It can both revoke and re-certify.

- [x] Publish a CRL revoking A's genuine certificate.
    > Correct: this is the first step described in the course for this attack.
- [x] Create a new certificate associating A with a public key whose private key it controls.
    > Correct: it can then impersonate A or intercept its communications (Man-in-the-Middle).
- [ ] Directly modify the content of messages already signed by A in the past.
    > Incorrect: compromising the CA's key does not make it possible to forge signatures already produced by A itself.
- [ ] Automatically become A's Registration Authority.
    > Incorrect: this is not a consequence mentioned in the course.


### What is the main purpose of the "separation of duties" principle between certification and revocation?

> Think about what makes the previous attack possible.

1. [ ] Reduce the CA's operating costs.
1. [x] Prevent a single compromised key from being able to both revoke a genuine certificate and issue a fake one.
    > Correct: by using distinct keys and entities (CA and Revocation Authority), compromising one does not compromise the other function.
1. [ ] Speed up the publication of certificates.


### What difference fundamentally distinguishes a Registration Authority from a Certification Authority?

> One requires direct contact with users, the other does not.

1. [ ] The Registration Authority signs certificates, the CA merely verifies identities.
1. [x] The Registration Authority performs the checks requiring direct contact with entities (identity, PoP), while the CA handles certificate creation/maintenance, often remotely.
    > Correct: this separation is generally motivated by geographic considerations.
1. [ ] They fulfill exactly the same role but in different jurisdictions.


### What are the main advantage and disadvantage of delegating key pair generation to a Key Generator?

> Who else then knows the user's private key?

1. [ ] Advantage: security enhancement only. Disadvantage: very high cost.
1. [x] Advantage: simplicity for the user and potentially enhanced security. Disadvantage: loss of non-repudiation, since the private key is known to a third party.
    > Correct: this is exactly the trade-off identified in the course.
1. [ ] Advantage: no private key is needed. Disadvantage: incompatibility with CAs.


### Do a Timestamp Agent and a Notary Agent fulfill exactly the same role?

> The TA certifies existence at a given moment; does the Notary Agent go further?

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: the Notary Agent additionally certifies the validity, origin, or ownership of the document, in support of non-repudiation, which the TA alone does not necessarily do.


### What is the main difference between the Clipper chip and its successor, the Capstone chip?

> Think about the type of cryptography used and the associated hardware medium.

1. [ ] The Clipper chip is asymmetric, the Capstone chip is symmetric.
1. [x] The Capstone chip brings asymmetric cryptography and can be integrated into a PCMCIA card (Fortezza) for military-level security use.
    > Correct: the Clipper chip (1993) was symmetric; its flaws and the need for asymmetric cryptography led to the Capstone chip.
1. [ ] The two systems are identical, only the commercial name changes.


### In a generic X.509 certificate, which field guarantees the authenticity of all the other information it contains?

> Which field covers all the preceding records?

1. [ ] Subject Public Key
1. [ ] Issuer
1. [x] Signature
    > Correct: the signature, computed with the CA's private key over all the preceding fields, guarantees the integrity and authenticity of the certificate.
1. [ ] Serial Number


### An application receives a certificate whose serial number appears in the latest CRL published by the issuing CA. What should it do?

> The primary purpose of a CRL is precisely to flag this kind of case.

1. [x] Consider the certificate invalid, even if it has not yet expired according to its Validity field.
    > Correct: presence in the CRL signals a revocation (e.g. compromised key), regardless of the original expiration date.
1. [ ] Trust the certificate as long as its Validity period has not elapsed.
1. [ ] Contact the Subject directly to ask for confirmation.


### Does using certificates with a very short validity period (requiring frequent re-confirmation) solve the revocation problem without introducing any new drawback?

> What then happens to the CA's operating mode?

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: this solution brings the system back to on-line mode, requiring high availability from the CA — the very drawback one was trying to avoid with the off-line mode.


### In an authentication tree, to verify the authenticity of leaf Y1 (with 4 leaves in total), which values must be provided in addition to Y1 itself?

> Which branches are not on the direct path from Y1 to the root?

- [x] h(Y2)
    > Correct: needed to recompute h1 = h(h(Y1) concatenated with h(Y2)).
- [ ] Y2 in plaintext
    > Incorrect: only the hashed value h(Y2) is needed, not the plaintext value.
- [x] h2 (the label of the internal node grouping Y3 and Y4)
    > Correct: needed to recompute the root R = h(h1 concatenated with h2).
- [ ] The CA's private key
    > Incorrect: no CA is involved in an authentication tree; only the root R needs to be authenticated separately (e.g. via a signature).


### What is the main advantage of an authentication tree compared to a classic certificate system?

> How many elements require direct cryptographic protection (a signature) in each system?

1. [ ] It completely eliminates the need for hash functions.
1. [x] Only the root R requires cryptographic protection; the rest of the values are protected by the non-reversibility of the hash function.
    > Correct: this is the main advantage identified in the course, unlike certificates where each record is directly signed.
1. [ ] It never requires recomputation, even in case of modification.
    > Incorrect: on the contrary, modifying a node requires recomputing the entire path to the root.


### Put the steps for constructing an authentication tree for n public values Y1...Yn back in order.

> Start with where the data is placed, then how the labels propagate up to the root.

1. Each non-terminal node with underlying arcs labeled h1 and h2 is labeled h(h1 concatenated with h2).
2. The values Y1, Y2, ..., Yn are placed in the leaves of the tree.
3. Each arc leaving a leaf Yi is labeled h(Yi).


### Why are balanced trees generally preferred for authentication trees?

> Think about the number of intermediate values needed to verify a leaf.

1. [ ] Because they make it possible to completely avoid recomputation upon modification.
1. [x] Because they reduce the number of intermediate values needed for verification, to the order of log2(n) rather than n.
    > Correct: a balanced tree minimizes the length of the path between a leaf and the root.
1. [ ] Because they make it possible to do without a collision-resistant hash function.


### Two different CAs, CA_A and CA_B, have established a cross-certificate CA_A{CA_B}. A wants to verify B's public key, certified by CA_B. What must B provide to A to complete the certification chain?

> The complete chain must allow A to trace back to a key it already authentically knows.

1. [ ] CA_B's private key.
1. [x] Its certificate signed by CA_B, namely CA_B{B}.
    > Correct: the chain CA_A{CA_B} · CA_B{B} allows A to verify B's key starting from its authentic copy of pub CA_A.
1. [ ] A new cross-certificate signed by CA_A.


### What structural difference sets the strict hierarchical model (PEM/X.509) apart from the trust graph model (PGP)?

> In one, there is a single starting point recognized by everyone; in the other, there is not.

1. [ ] The PGP model imposes a single root known worldwide, unlike PEM/X.509.
1. [x] PEM/X.509 relies on a single root whose key is known to everyone, whereas PGP relies on a graph in which the users themselves act as CAs for their correspondents.
    > Correct: this difference explains why PGP is well suited to closed groups but limited for unconnected populations, unlike the hierarchical model.
1. [ ] The two models are structurally identical, only the terminology differs.


### Is a certification chain always as secure as its strongest link?

> Think about what happens if just one intermediate certificate in the chain is compromised.

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: the course states that a certification chain is as vulnerable as its weakest link, which is why chains should be kept as short as possible.


### Does the "Key Backup and Recovery" functionality of a PKI apply equally to signing and decryption private keys?

> The course specifies an important nuance on this point.

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: this procedure applies mainly to the decryption private key; backing up a signing private key would create a non-repudiation problem.


### A company deploying a complete PKI hopes to avoid "case-by-case" security solutions. What advantages does this directly bring it, according to the course?

> Think about the integration of several security services into a single environment.

- [x] Integrated management of several services: strong authentication, signature/non-repudiation, single sign-on, VPN, secure B2B/B2C communications.
    > Correct: this is the "all in one" advantage described in the course, a source of savings compared to separate solutions.
- [x] Easier interoperability thanks to widely used standards (X.509, PKCS, OCSP).
    > Correct: compliance with these standards fosters compatibility both within and between companies.
- [ ] A guaranteed reduction in implementation cost compared to any other solution.
    > Incorrect: the course instead identifies implementation cost as a major disadvantage of PKIs.
- [ ] The complete elimination of the need for qualified personnel.
    > Incorrect: the course instead mentions the scarcity of skills as a disadvantage.

title: Information System Security
text:
Digital Signatures: Definitions

Digital signature: string of data allowing a message (in digital form) to be associated with an originating entity.
Digital signature scheme: generation algorithm + verification algorithm.
Signature process: message formatting + signature generation algorithm
Verification process: verification algorithm + (message reconstruction).
Classification of digital signatures:

Digital signatures with appendix which require the presence of the original message to verify the validity of the signature. These are the most commonly used. Examples: ElGamal, DSS.
Digital signatures with message recovery which additionally offer the possibility of reconstructing the message from the signature. Examples: RSA, Rabin.

Digital signatures are mostly based on asymmetric cryptography because the notion of a shared key is not suited to the need to explicitly identify an entity.
Commitments similar to those obtained with a public-key signature (such as non-repudiation of origin) can nevertheless be obtained with symmetric technology and trusted third parties (Trusted Third Parties or TTP). These methods are called: arbitrated digital signatures.

title: Information System Security
section: Digital Signatures with Appendix: Formal Framework
text:
Digital Signatures with Appendix: Formal Framework

We assume that each entity has a private key to sign messages and an authentic copy of the public keys of its correspondents.

Notation:

\(M\): Message space
\(M_h\): \(m_h = H(m)\) with \(m \in M\), \(m_h \in M_h\) and \(H\) a hash function
\(S\): Space of values that can be obtained by a signature process

Description:
Each entity defines an injective map \(S_A : M_h \to S\) ; (i.e. the signature)
The map \(S_A\) gives rise to a map \(V_A\):
\[V_A: M_h \times S \to \{\text{true}, \text{false}\}\] ; (i.e. the verification)
s.t. \(\forall\ m_h \in M_h, s \in S\), we have:
\[V_A(m_h, s) = \text{true if } S_A(m_h) = s \text{ and}\] \[V_A(m_h, s) = \text{false otherwise}\]
The \(S_A\) operations require A’s private key while the \(V_A\) operations use A’s public key.

Some simple properties:

The \(S_A\) and \(V_A\) operations must be easy to compute (given the corresponding keys)
It is (computationally) infeasible for an entity not having A’s private key to find an \(m'\) and an \(s'\) with \(m' \in M\) and \(s' \in S\) s.t. \(V_A(m'_h, s') = \text{true}\) with \(m'_h = H(m')\).

title: Information System Security
section: DS with message recovery: Formal Framework
text:
DS with message recovery: Formal Framework
Notation: in addition to the previous definitions, we have:

\(M_s\): The space of elements to which a signature can be applied.
\(R\): An injective map: \(M \to M_s\), called the redundancy function. It must be invertible and public.
\(M_R\): \(M_R = \text{Im}(R)\)

Description:
Each entity defines an injective map \(S_A : M_S \to S\) ; (i.e. the signature)
The map \(S_A\) gives rise to a map \(V_A\): ; (i.e. the verification)
\[V_A : S \to M_s \text{, s.t. } V_A \circ S_A = \text{Identity on } M_s\]
Note that verification is performed without A’s private key
Signature generation:

Compute \(m_R = R(m)\) and \(s = S_A(m_R)\)
Publish \(s\) as A’s signature on \(m\). This allows other entities to verify the signature and reconstruct \(m\).

Verification:

Compute \(m_R = V_A(s)\) (with A’s public key)
Check that \(m_R \in M_R\) (otherwise reject the signature)
Reconstruct \(m\) by computing: \(R^{-1}(m_R)\)

title: Information System Security
text:
DS with message recovery: Properties

Properties:

The \(S_A\) and \(V_A\) operations must be easy to compute (given the corresponding keys)
It is (computationally) infeasible for an entity not having A’s private key to find an \(s' \in S\) s.t. \(V_A(s') \notin M_R\)

Remarks on the redundancy function:

The choice of a redundancy function is essential for the security of the system.
If \(M_R = M_S\) and \(R\) and \(S_A\) are bijections from \(M\) to \(M_R\) and from \(M_S\) to \(S\) respectively, then \(M\) and \(S\) have the same size and, consequently, it is trivial to forge messages bearing A’s signature.

Example of a redundancy function: let \(M = \{m: m \in \{0,1\}^n\}\) (n being the message size) and \(M_S = \{t: t \in \{0,1\}^{2n}\}\). Let \(R : M \to M_S\) s.t. \(R(m) = m \| m\) ( \(\|\) being the concatenation of 2 messages). The probability of landing on such a message when trying to forge a message from a signature is: \(|M_R| / |M_S| = (1/2)^n\), which is negligible for large messages.
Warning!: A redundancy function suited to one digital signature scheme may cause flaws in a different one!

title: Information System Security
text:
RSA Signature Process1
Key Generation

Each entity (A) creates a key pair (public and private) as follows:

A chooses the size of the modulus n (e.g. size(n) = 1024 or size(n) = 2048).
A generates two large prime numbers p and q (\(\sim n/2\) in size).
A computes \(n := pq\) and \(\Phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1)\).
A generates the verification exponent e, with \(1 < e < \Phi(n)\) s.t. \(\text{gcd}(e, \Phi(n)) = 1\).
A computes the signature exponent d, s.t.: \(ed \equiv 1 \bmod \Phi(n)\) using the extended Euclidean algorithm or the fast exponentiation algorithm (page 94).
The pair (n,e) is A’s public key; d is A’s private key.


Signature

A computes the redundancy function of the message m: \(m_R := R(m)\).
A computes the signature: \(s := m_R^{\ d} \bmod n\) and sends s to B.

Verification

Entity B obtains (n,e), A’s authentic public key.
B computes \(m'_R = s^e \bmod n\), checks \(m'_R \in M_R\) and rejects the signature if \(m'_R \notin M_R\).
B recovers the message correctly signed by A by computing: \(m = R^{-1}(m'_R)\).

title: Information System Security
text:
RSA Signature: Remarks

The proof of correctness is identical to that of the encryption process (page 99). The order of exponentiation has no effect since:

\[ed \equiv de \equiv 1 \bmod \Phi(n)\]

The process can also be used to produce signatures with appendix with the following modifications:

Signature:

A uses a hash function H and computes \(m_h := H(m)\).
A computes the signature of \(m_h\): \(s := m_h^{\ d} \bmod n\) and sends the pair (m,s) to B.

Verification

B computes \(m'_h = s^e \bmod n\) and \(H(m)\) and checks the equality \(m'_h = H(m)\).
If the equality holds, B accepts the signature s of A on the message M.
Signature computation is slower than verification because of the size difference between the exponent d (\(\text{size}(d) \approx \text{size}(\Phi(n))\)) and e.
The risks and attacks mentioned in the encryption process (page 102) also apply to the signature.
Encryption and signature key pairs should be kept distinct since they require separate storage, backup, and update policies.

title: Information System Security
text:
“Blind” Signatures (Blind Signatures)

Scheme invented by Chaum (Chau822).
Idea: A sends information to B for signature. B returns the signed information to A. From this signature, A can compute B’s signature on another message chosen beforehand by A. This allows A to obtain a signature from B on a message that B has never seen (hence the name blind signature…)
In fact, this is a flaw based on the multiplicative property of RSA (page 102) that was exploited to create a new signature process.
Algorithm: Let \(S_B\) be B’s RSA signature with (n,e) and d, respectively B’s public and private keys. Let k be a fixed integer with \(\text{gcd}(n,k) = 1\):

\[f: \mathbb{Z}_n \to \mathbb{Z}_n \text{ with } f(m) = m \cdot k^e \bmod n\] ; blinding function
\[g: \mathbb{Z}_n \to \mathbb{Z}_n \text{ with } g(m) = k^{-1} \cdot m \bmod n\] ; unblinding function
which gives:
\[g(S_B(f(m))) = g(S_B(mk^e \bmod n)) = g(m^d k \bmod n) = m^d \bmod n = S_B(m) \quad (*)\]

Protocol:

\[A \to B: m' = f(m)\] \[A \leftarrow B: s' = S_B(m')\]
A computes \(g(s')\) and obtains the desired signature using (*).

title: Information System Security
text:
Rabin Signature Process3
Key Generation

Each entity (A) creates a key pair (public and private) as follows:

A generates two large random prime numbers p and q (\(len(pq) \geq 1024\)).
A computes \(n := pq\).
A’s public key is n, A’s private key is (p,q).


Signature

A computes the redundancy function of the message m: \(m_R := R(m)\).
A uses its private key to compute the signature: \(s := m_R^{1/2} \bmod n\) using efficient algorithms for computing square roots mod p and mod q.
A sends s to B (s is one of 4 square roots obtained).

Verification

Entity B obtains n, A’s authentic public key.
B computes \(m'_R = s^2 \bmod n\), checks \(m'_R \in M_R\) and rejects the signature if \(m'_R \notin M_R\).
B recovers the message correctly signed by A by computing: \(m = R^{-1}(m'_R)\).

title: Information System Security
text:
ElGamal Signature Process4
Key Generation

Each entity (A) creates a key pair (public and private) as follows:

A generates a prime number p (\(len(p) \geq 1024\) bits) and a generator \(\alpha\) of \(\mathbb{Z}_p^{*}\).
A generates a random number a, s.t. \(1 \leq a \leq p-2\) and computes \(y := \alpha^a \bmod p\).
A’s public key is \((p, \alpha, y)\), A’s private key is a.


Signature

A uses a hash function H and computes \(m_h := H(m).\)
A generates a random number k (\(1 \leq k \leq p-2\) and \(\text{gcd}(k,p-1) = 1\)) and computes \(k^{-1} \bmod (p-1)\)
A computes \(r := \alpha^k \bmod p\) and then \(s := k^{-1} (m_h - ar) \bmod (p-1)\)
A’s signature on the message m is the pair (r,s).

Verification

Entity B obtains \((p, \alpha, \alpha^a \bmod p)\), A’s authentic public key.
B checks that \(1 \leq r \leq p-2\), otherwise rejects the signature.
B computes \(v_1 := y^r r^s \bmod p\).
B computes \(H(m)\) and \(v_2 := \alpha^{H(m)} \bmod p\)
B accepts the signature iff. \(v_1 = v_2\).

title: Information System Security
text:
ElGamal Signature: Remarks

Proof that the scheme works: If \(s \equiv k^{-1} (m_h - ar) \bmod (p-1)\), we have that:

\[m_h \equiv (ar + ks) \bmod (p-1) \text{ and}\] \[v_2 = \alpha^{H(m)} \bmod p\]
if, as we wish to show \(m_h = H(m)\), by reducing the exponents mod (p-1) (page 92), we can rewrite \(v_2\):
\[v_2 \equiv \alpha^{ar+ks} \bmod p\]
On the other hand:
\[v_1 = y^r r^s \equiv \alpha^{ar} \alpha^{ks} \equiv \alpha^{ar+ks} \bmod p \qquad \text{q.e.d.}\]

By construction, the ElGamal scheme works only with appendix (the result of applying a hash function). The Nyberg-Rueppel scheme5 introduces a variation allowing message recovery.
The Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA), approved by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, has become the most commonly used signature standard. It is built as a direct derivative of the ElGamal scheme with the SHA-1 hash function (page 128).

Most cryptocurrencies are based on asymmetric cryptography. Bitcoin, for example, uses digital signatures to authenticate its transactions
Spending or transmitting bitcoins requires signing with the private key of the holder (who was in turn the recipient of the previous transaction):




Source Image: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System. Satoshi Nakamoto



Bitcoin and Ethereum use the ECDSA algorithm (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) derived from the ElGamal signature algorithm on elliptic curves, whose security relies on ECDLP (page 109).

Types of attacks on DS

Criteria for “breaking” a digital signature scheme:

Total Break: Computing the signer’s private key or an efficient (polynomial) algorithm for generating signatures.
Selective forgery. The adversary is able to generate a valid signature for a fixed message (or class of messages).
Existential forgery. The adversary is able to forge a signature for (at least) one message (over which it has no control).

Basic attacks:

Key-only attacks: The adversary has knowledge only of the signer’s public key.
Message-based attacks: The adversary has access to signatures corresponding to:

known-messages
chosen-messages
adaptive chosen-messages


Equivalent to x-ciphertext attacks but with messages!

title: Information System Security
text:
Fundamental concepts 🔴

Digital signature: string of data linking a message to an originating entity.
Signature scheme = generation algorithm + verification algorithm.
Signature process = message formatting + signature generation.
Verification process = verification algorithm + (message reconstruction).
Based on asymmetric cryptography (a shared key does not allow an entity to be explicitly identified).
Arbitrated digital signatures: symmetric equivalent, via a TTP (Trusted Third Party).


Two families

WarningPitfall



Don’t confuse: “with appendix” = the message is kept alongside the signature; “with recovery” = the signature contains the message (via an invertible redundancy function).

title: Information System Security
text:
Formal framework 🟠
With appendix:

\(S_A : M_h \to S\) (signature, private key)
\(V_A : M_h \times S \to \{\text{true,false}\}\) (verification, public key)
\(m_h = H(m)\)

With recovery:

\(R : M \to M_S\): redundancy function, injective, invertible and public
\(S_A : M_S \to S\), then \(V_A : S \to M_s\) s.t. \(V_A \circ S_A = \text{Id}\)
Verification without A’s private key
Steps: (1) \(m_R = R(m)\), \(s = S_A(m_R)\) → (2) check \(V_A(s) \in M_R\) → (3) \(m = R^{-1}(m_R)\)







ImportantKey takeaway



The choice of R is critical: if \(M_R = M_S\) and \(R\), \(S_A\) are bijections, \(M\) and \(S\) have the same size → it becomes trivial to forge signed messages.

Attacks on digital signatures 🔴
Breaking levels (from most to least severe):

Total Break: recovering the private key or a polynomial-time signature generation algorithm.
Selective forgery: signing a message (or class) fixed in advance.

Attack

title: Information System Security
text:
Key takeaways

Signature = one-way function invertible only with the private key; verification = public operation.
Appendix (ElGamal/DSS) vs Recovery (RSA/Rabin): the key difference is the presence/absence of a redundancy function \(R\) allowing \(m\) to be recovered.
RSA/Rabin: security = factorization (RSAP/SQROOTP); ElGamal/DSA/ECDSA: security = discrete logarithm (DLP/ECDLP).
Rabin produces 4 candidate signatures per message.
Blind signature = exploitation of RSA’s multiplicative property.
Bitcoin/Ethereum: signatures = ECDSA, transaction chaining via hash + successive signature/verification.
Breaking a signature: Total Break > Selective forgery > Existential forgery; adversary access: key-only < known < chosen < adaptive chosen.
