title: Information System Security
text:
Data Origin Authentication
Goal: prove that \(X\) comes from \(A\) (symmetric key \(k\) shared by \(A,B\)).









##
Protocol
Formula
Property




1
MAC
\(A\to B: X,\ \mathrm{MAC}_k(X)\)
integrity + origin


2
MDC + encryption
\(A\to B: X,\ E_k(\mathrm{MDC}(X))\)
same, without a dedicated MAC key


3
MDC + encryption (confidential)
\(A\to B: E_k(X,\mathrm{MDC}(X))\)
+ confidentiality of \(X\)


4
MDC + signature
\(A\to B: X,\ \mathrm{Sig}_{priv\text{-}A}(\mathrm{MDC}(X))\)
+ non-repudiation









WarningPitfall



These 4 protocols guarantee neither uniqueness nor freshness (timeliness): they are vulnerable to replay attacks. Time/context-aware mechanisms are needed (→ entity authentication).

title: Information System Security
text:
Entity Authentication: Fundamental Concepts
Terminology: user/A = claimant (proves its identity); system/B = verifier (verifies).
Possible proof elements:

something known: password, PIN, private/secret key.
something possessed: passport, smart card, password generator.
something inherent: biometrics (fingerprints, retina, DNA).

4 objectives of a robust protocol:

If \(A,B\) are honest and \(A\) is authenticated → \(B\) accepts.
\(B\) cannot reuse \(A\)’s information to impersonate \(A\) to \(C\).
The probability that a third party \(C\) impersonates \(A\) to \(B\) = negligible.
Point 3 remains true even if \(C\) has observed/participated in numerous past instances, including in parallel.










Satisfies
Secret revealed?




Weak authentication
1, 3
yes (password transmitted)


Strong authentication
1, 2, 3, 4 (at least partially)
no (proof of possession)


Zero-Knowledge
strong + nothing about the secret
no, no information

title: Information System Security
text:
Cross-Cutting Attacks and Properties
Dictionary attack: word database (+ variants) tested against a hashing/encryption system to recover passwords/keys.

Offline: from the database of hashed passwords, or from a pair \((R, E_p(R))\) observed passively (e.g.: \(A\to B: A\) ; \(B\to A: R\) ; \(A\to B: E_p(R)\)).
Online: less effective (systems limit unsuccessful attempts).

Plaintext-equivalence: a piece of data is plaintext-equivalent to a password \(p\) if it grants the same access as \(p\).

E.g.: if \(A\to B: H(p)\), then \(H(p)\) is plaintext-equivalent to \(p\) → hashing at storage time alone adds nothing if it is \(H(p)\) that transits.
UNIX /etc/passwd: it is \(p\) (not \(H(p)\)) that is exchanged → the stored hash is not plaintext-equivalent.
Ideal: neither plaintext-equivalent, nor exposed to offline dictionary attacks.







WarningPitfall



Hashing a password at storage time does not protect against an attack if it is the hash itself that is sent to the server to authenticate (it becomes the equivalent of the password).

title: Information System Security
text:
Weak Authentication
Fixed password (independent of time/number of executions):

Storage in the clear → risk: OS flaws, super-user, backups.
Hashed storage (one-way function), possibly public (UNIX) → risk: offline attacks (guessing, brute-force, collisions).
Protections: robustness rules (entropy), slow down/limit attempts, salting, restrict distribution of the file.
Major problem: replayable after network eavesdropping (replay).

Variable password: the password changes with time/number of executions.
One-time password — Lamport scheme (S/Key):

Init: \(A\) chooses secret \(w\), constant \(t\) (~1000), OWF \(H\); \(A\to B: w_t = H^t(w)\); \(B\) stores \(w_{stored}=w_t,\ n=t-1\).
Identification \((t-n)\): \(A\to B: A\); \(B\to A: n\); \(A\to B: w_n = H^n(w)\).
\(B\) checks \(H(w_n) == w_{stored}\); if OK, \(n\mathrel{-}=1\), \(w_{stored}:=w_n\).
Ends when \(n=0\) → new secret \(w\).







WarningPitfall



Authenticating \(B\) is necessary, otherwise \(C\) impersonates \(B\):

pre-play attack: \(C\) obtains the current \(w_n\) and replays it.
small-n attack: \(C\) supplies a smaller \(n\) → can recompute all the \(H^{m>n}(w_n)\).



Hardware generators (SecurID/RSA): card generates a different number every 30–60 s (secret key + clock), combined with a PIN. Exposed to pre-play but with a window limited to 30–60 s.
Conclusion: fixed password = very low security; variable password = a step toward strong authentication but requires precautions.

title: Information System Security
text:
Strong Authentication — Symmetric Solutions
Shared key \(k_{AB}\). General principle = challenge and response.
Unilateral (challenge-response), v1: \(A\to B: A\) ; \(B\to A: R\) ; \(A\to B: E_{k_{AB}}(R)\) — \(B\) decrypts and compares.

Improvement vs. password: randomness \(R\) prevents direct replay.
Residual risks: known/chosen-plaintext offline (not very effective if the encryption is secure); active MitM if \(B\) is not authenticated.
\(E_{k_{AB}}(R)\) can be replaced by an MDC \(H(k_{AB},R)\) or MAC \(H_{k_{AB}}(R)\) (faster).

Unilateral, v2 (timestamp): \(A\to B: A, E_{k_{AB}}(\text{timestamp})\).

Advantage: one fewer message, stateless.
Limit: requires synchronized clocks → exploitable “drift”; advancing \(B\)’s clock can revalidate old instances.

Bilateral, naive solution: \(A\to B: A,R_2\) ; \(B\to A: R_1, E_{k_{AB}}(R_2)\) ; \(A\to B: E_{k_{AB}}(R_1)\).






WarningPitfall — reflection attack



\(C\) opens two instances in parallel with \(B\): it uses the \(R_1\) received in instance 2 as the encrypted answer to supply in instance 1 (mirroring the challenge). \(C\) never needs to know \(k_{AB}\).


Bilateral, robust solution: \(A\to B: A,R_2\) ; \(B\to A: E_{k_{AB}}(R_1,R_2,A)\) ; \(A\to B: E_{k_{AB}}(R_2,R_1)\).

Including the recipient’s identity (\(A\) or \(B\)) in the encrypted message prevents reflection (mirroring toward another target is detected).
Including \(R_1\) in the encrypted part also protects against chosen-plaintext attacks.

title: Information System Security
text:
Strong Authentication — Asymmetric Solutions
Unilateral, naive: \(A\to B: A\) ; \(B\to A: E_{pub\text{-}A}(R)\) ; \(A\to B: R\).






WarningPitfall



\(B\) can mount a chosen-ciphertext attack: it has \(A\) decrypt anything by passing it off as \(R\).


Unilateral, robust (structure + redundancy): \(A\to B: A\) ; \(B\to A: H(R), B, E_{pub\text{-}A}(B,R)\).

\(A\) decrypts, checks \(H(R')=H(R)\) and \(B'=B\), otherwise suspends; then \(A\to B: R\).
A dual variant is possible with a signature (\(priv\text{-}A\)) instead of encryption.

Bilateral — Needham-Schroeder: \((1)\ A\to B: E_{pub\text{-}B}(r_1,A)\) ; \((2)\ B\to A: E_{pub\text{-}A}(r_1,r_2)\) ; \((3)\ A\to B: r_2\).

Including \(A\) in \((1)\) counters chosen-ciphertext attacks.
Possible reinforcement: add a witness \(H(r_1)\) in \((1)\).

title: Information System Security
text:
Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKIP)
Motivation: in classical methods, \(B\) (or an observer) learns something about the secret (the whole password, or exploitable plaintext/ciphertext pairs).
Proof of knowledge (proof of knowledge) — 2 properties:

Completeness: \(A,B\) honest → \(B\) accepts \(A\)’s proof.
Soundness: a dishonest \(C\) who fools \(B\) ⟹ \(C\) possesses the secret (or polynomially equivalent information).

ZKIP = proof of knowledge + zero-knowledge: \(A\) convinces \(B\) without revealing any information about the secret.

Computational ZKIP: indistinguishable by a probabilistic-polynomial observer.
Perfect ZKIP: indistinguishable in the strict probabilistic sense (Shannon’s theory).

Generic structure (repeated \(n\) times):

\(A\to B\): witness — commitment to a class of questions.
\(B\to A\): challenge — random question within this class.
\(A\to B\): response — via the secret.







TipIntuition — the cave



\(A\) knows the secret passage between \(y\) and \(z\). \(B\) waits at the entrance \(x\), \(A\) enters via \(y\) or \(z\) (witness), \(B\) asks \(A\) to come back out on a specific side (challenge). \(A\) obeys thanks to the secret (response). Repeated \(n\) times: an impostor has a \(2^{-n}\) chance of fooling \(B\) each time. Analogous to cut-and-choose (sharing a pie).



Graph Isomorphism

\(G_1,G_2\) are isomorphic if there exists \(\pi\) s.t. \(\{u,v\}\in E_1 \iff \{\pi(u),\pi(v)\}\in E_2\).
Easy to compute \(\pi\) when knowing both graphs; hard to determine whether two large graphs (~1000 vertices) are isomorphic without the secret.
Protocol: \(A\) publishes \(G_1,G_2\) (secret \(\pi\)). Witness \(H=\delta(G_2)\); challenge \(i\in\{1,2\}\); response \(\lambda\) s.t. \(H=\lambda(G_i)\) (\(\lambda=\delta\) if \(i=2\), \(\lambda=\delta\circ\pi\) if \(i=1\)). \(B\) checks \(H=\lambda(G_i)\).
Little used in practice (inefficient to implement).



Fiat-Shamir Algorithm
Goal: prove knowledge of \(s\) without revealing it, a basis for real implementations.
Init: trusted third party \(T\) publishes \(n=pq\) (keeps \(p,q\) secret). \(A\) chooses \(s\) (with \(\gcd(s,n)=1\)), publishes \(v=s^2 \bmod n\) (certified by \(T\)).
\((1)\ A\to B: x=r^2\bmod n\) (witness, \(r\) random) \((2)\ B\to A: e\in\{0,1\}\) (challenge) \((3)\ A\to B: y = r\cdot s^e \bmod n\) (response)
\(B\) rejects if \(y=0\); accepts if \(y^2 \equiv x\cdot v^e \pmod n\). Repeated until sufficient confidence is reached.







Property
Justification




Completeness
\(A\) knows \(s\) → proof always accepted


Soundness
Without \(s\), an impostor can only answer a single challenge (0 or 1) without breaking SQROOTP


Zero-Knowledge
\(s\) is masked by the random blinding factor \(r\) when \(e=1\)


Perfect ZK
\(B\) alone can simulate pairs \((x,y)\) of the same distribution





Common Implementations








Protocol
Basis
Particularity




Feige-Fiat-Shamir (FFS)
Fiat-Shamir
multiple witnesses/challenges (\(k\) values) → probability \(2^{-nk}\)


Guillou-Quisquater (GQ)
Fiat-Shamir
widened challenge domain, fewer instances needed


Schnorr
discrete logarithm (DLP)
only 3 exchanges; sometimes sacrifices ZK for efficiency



More efficient than RSA, suited to smart cards. Satisfy completeness + soundness; ZK is sometimes sacrificed for performance.






WarningPitfall — Mafia attack



Even a perfect ZKIP can be hijacked by a real-time relay: \(A\) interacts with \(C\) (accomplice) while its accomplice \(D\) relays the messages to an honest verifier \(B\), impersonating \(A\). The ZKIP proves knowledge of the secret at the moment of the protocol, not the physical identity of the party responding. Countermeasures: Faraday cage, strong synchronization.

title: Information System Security
text:
Summary — Attacks and Protections








Attack
Description
Protection




replay
replaying a previous instance
zero-knowledge ; challenge-response ; one-time password (watch out for pre-play)


known/chosen-plaintext
obtaining plaintext/ciphertext pairs
zero-knowledge


chosen-ciphertext
getting chosen data decrypted/signed
zero-knowledge ; challenge-response + witness + structure/redundancy


reflection
replying with the same number received
including the target entity in the messages ; asymmetry of the messages


interleaving
mixing messages from several instances
including the target entity ; cryptographic chaining between messages of one instance


collusion
connivance between the parties involved (Mafia)
Faraday cage ; strong synchronization

title: Information System Security
text:
Key Takeaways

Data origin ≠ entity identification: the former authenticates a one-off message, the latter authenticates an actor over time.
Weak = secret revealed (password); strong = proof of possession (challenge-response); ZK = proof with no information leakage whatsoever.
Every robust solution combines: non-reused randomness + recipient’s identity in the encrypted message + structure/redundancy.
Symmetric: risks = reflection, MitM if not mutual. Asymmetric: risk = chosen-ciphertext if poorly structured.
ZKIP relies on completeness + soundness + zero-knowledge, structured as witness → challenge → response, repeated to reduce the probability of cheating.
Even a perfect ZKIP does not protect against a real-time relay (Mafia attack): the protocol proves a secret, not a location.

title: Information System Security
text:
### Which statement correctly distinguishes a signature with appendix from a signature with message recovery?

> Think about what each type of verification needs as input.

1. [ ] A signature with appendix is always shorter than a signature with recovery.
1. [x] A signature with appendix requires the presence of the original message to be verified, unlike a signature with recovery, which allows the message to be retrieved from the signature itself.
    > Correct: this is precisely the distinction made in the course between the two classes of schemes.
1. [ ] A signature with recovery necessarily requires a hash function, unlike a signature with appendix.
    > Incorrect: the opposite is true in the course's examples (RSA and Rabin, with recovery, do not necessarily use hashing; ElGamal, with appendix, does use one).
1. [ ] Both classes offer exactly the same security guarantees and differ only in name.
    > Incorrect: they differ in the nature of the verification map and in what it allows to be recovered.


### In the formal framework of signatures with appendix, which statements about the maps $S_A$ and $V_A$ are correct?

> Review the definition of the spaces $M_h$, $S$ and the relationship between $S_A$ and $V_A$.

- [x] $S_A$ is an injective map from $M_h$ to $S$.
    > Correct: this is the definition given in the course for the signature.
- [x] $V_A$ requires A's public key, while $S_A$ requires A's private key.
    > Correct: the course explicitly specifies this separation of keys used.
- [ ] $V_A$ takes only $m_h$ as input and returns an element of $S$.
    > Incorrect: $V_A$ takes the pair $(m_h, s)$ as input and returns a boolean (true/false).
- [ ] It should be easy, even without A's private key, to find a pair $(m', s')$ such that $V_A(m'_h, s') = \text{true}$.
    > Incorrect: it's the opposite, this operation must be computationally infeasible without A's private key.


### Digital signatures are mostly based on symmetric cryptography, because the notion of a shared key is best suited to identifying an entity explicitly.

> Think about what it means to "share" a key between multiple entities.

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: the course states that digital signatures are mostly based on asymmetric cryptography, precisely because a shared key does not allow an entity to be identified explicitly.


### To which category of signatures do RSA and Rabin belong according to the course's classification?

> Go back to the list of examples given for each of the two signature classes.

1. [ ] Signatures with appendix, like ElGamal and DSS.
1. [x] Signatures with message recovery.
    > Correct: the course explicitly cites RSA and Rabin as examples of signatures with message recovery.
1. [ ] Blind signatures.
    > Incorrect: blind signatures form a distinct process, although derived from RSA.
1. [ ] Arbitrated digital signatures.
    > Incorrect: this category relies on symmetric cryptography and trusted third parties, not directly on RSA or Rabin.


### Put the steps of RSA signature key generation back in order.

> Think about what must be known before the signature exponent d can be computed.

1. Compute the signature exponent d such that ed ≡ 1 mod Φ(n)
2. Choose the size of the modulus n
3. Compute n = pq and Φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1)
4. Generate the verification exponent e coprime with Φ(n)
5. Generate two large prime numbers p and q


### When verifying an RSA signature with recovery, a student computes $m'_R = s^e \bmod n$ but omits checking that $m'_R \in M_R$ before reconstructing the message. What is the main risk of this omission?

> Think back to the role of the redundancy function in rejecting invalid signatures.

1. [ ] No risk: this check is merely a performance optimization, not a security measure.
    > Incorrect: the course explicitly states that the signature must be rejected if $m'_R \notin M_R$, it is not optional.
1. [x] An attacker could get an arbitrary value $s'$ accepted as a valid signature, since no check prevents reconstructing a message from a value that was never actually signed by A.
    > Correct: checking membership in $M_R$ is precisely what prevents an adversary without the private key from forging accepted signatures.
1. [ ] The reconstructed message would systematically be longer than the original message.
    > Incorrect: this is not the consequence described in the course; it is a security issue, not a size issue.
1. [ ] This only affects the speed of computing the signature, not its verification.
    > Incorrect: the omission concerns the verification step itself, not signature generation.


### Why is the choice of the redundancy function R described as essential for the security of a signature scheme with message recovery?

> Think about what would happen if almost every value in $M_S$ belonged to $M_R$.

1. [ ] Because R determines the size of the private key used to sign.
    > Incorrect: the size of the private key depends on the choice of n, p and q, not on R.
1. [x] Because if $M_R$ is too close in size to $M_S$, it becomes easy to arbitrarily choose a value in $M_S$ that belongs to $M_R$, which would allow a signature to be forged without knowing the private key.
    > Correct: the course illustrates this point with the example where $M_R = M_S$ makes forgery trivial.
1. [ ] Because R must remain secret for the scheme to be secure.
    > Incorrect: the course states on the contrary that R must be public and invertible.
1. [ ] Because R entirely replaces the role of the public key in verification.
    > Incorrect: R and the public key play distinct and complementary roles.


### If $M_R = M_S$ and both $R$ and $S_A$ are bijections, what direct consequence does this have for the security of the scheme?

> Compare the size of M and S in this particular case.

1. [ ] The scheme becomes more secure, because each message has a unique signature.
    > Incorrect: uniqueness of the signature does not prevent forgery here.
1. [x] M and S have the same size, which makes it trivial to forge messages bearing A's signature.
    > Correct: this is exactly the course's remark on this particular case.
1. [ ] Verification becomes impossible without A's private key.
    > Incorrect: it's the opposite that is problematic, verification (and therefore forgery) becomes too easy.
1. [ ] This has no particular effect as long as the hash function remains secure.
    > Incorrect: this case doesn't even involve the use of a hash function; it is a structural flaw in R.


### In a scheme with message recovery, which statements about the verification map $V_A$ are correct?

> Go back to the definition of $V_A$ given in the formal framework with recovery.

- [x] $V_A$ satisfies $V_A \circ S_A = \text{Identity}$ on $M_s$.
    > Correct: this is the fundamental property that allows the message to be reconstructed.
- [x] Verification is performed without A's private key.
    > Correct: the course states this explicitly, unlike some generation operations.
- [ ] $V_A$ takes the original message m as input and returns the signature s.
    > Incorrect: it's the opposite, $V_A$ takes s as input and allows $m_R$ and then m to be recovered.
- [ ] $V_A$ always requires a hash function to work.
    > Incorrect: this formal framework does not introduce a hash function, unlike the variant with appendix.


### An adversary, without knowing A's private key, manages to find a pair $(m', s')$ such that $V_A(m'_h, s') = \text{true}$. What does this situation reveal about the expected properties of the scheme?

> Go back to the simple property regarding computational infeasibility in the formal framework with appendix.

1. [ ] Nothing abnormal: this situation is expected and accepted by the scheme as long as m' is different from the original message.
    > Incorrect: the course explicitly states that it must be infeasible to find such a pair without the private key.
1. [x] The scheme violates the fundamental security property expected, since it should be computationally infeasible to produce such a pair without A's private key.
    > Correct: this property is precisely what guarantees that only A can produce valid signatures.
1. [ ] This simply means A reused the same public key for two different messages.
    > Incorrect: reuse of the public key is not the issue here, it is the infeasibility-of-forgery property that is violated.
1. [ ] This only proves that the hash function H used is poorly chosen.
    > Incorrect: the problem concerns the $S_A$/$V_A$ map itself, not necessarily the choice of H.


### Why is computing an RSA signature slower than verifying it?

> Compare the typical size of the signature exponent d to that of the verification exponent e.

1. [ ] Because signing requires generating new prime numbers p and q each time.
    > Incorrect: p and q are generated only once when the key pair is created, not for every signature.
1. [x] Because the size of the signature exponent d is comparable to that of Φ(n), while the verification exponent e can be chosen to be much smaller.
    > Correct: this is exactly the course's remark on the size difference between d and e.
1. [ ] Because verification does not use modular exponentiation, unlike signing.
    > Incorrect: both operations rely on modular exponentiation, only the exponent size differs.
1. [ ] Because signing requires a public key while verification does not.
    > Incorrect: it's the opposite: signing uses the private key, verification uses the public key.


### In the RSA variant with appendix, what is the role of the hash function H?

> Think about what is actually signed, and what distinguishes this variant from the basic RSA scheme with a redundancy function.

1. [ ] It entirely replaces the role of the signature exponent d.
    > Incorrect: H and d play distinct roles; d remains essential for computing the signature.
1. [x] It produces a fixed-size digest $m_h = H(m)$, which is signed instead of the full message, thus avoiding the direct application of a redundancy function to the entire message.
    > Correct: this is what the course describes for the RSA-with-appendix version, where (m,s) is sent and B recomputes H(m) to verify.
1. [ ] It is used only to compress the message to reduce bandwidth, with no link to security.
    > Incorrect: its role is directly linked to signature generation and verification, not just compression.
1. [ ] It allows B to fully reconstruct the message m from the signature s.
    > Incorrect: with appendix, B already has direct access to m; it is not the signature that allows it to be reconstructed.


### The security of the RSA signature process relies on a different mathematical problem than that of RSA encryption.

> The course explicitly refers to the proof of the encryption process to justify why the signature works.

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: the course states that the proof of correctness of the signature is identical to that of the encryption process, and the summary table associates RSA with the same underlying problem (RSAP) for both uses.


### Put the steps of Chaum's blind signature protocol back in order.

> Think about what A must do before sending anything to B, and then what A does after receiving B's reply.

1. A computes g(s') to obtain the unblinded signature on m
2. A computes m' = f(m) using the blinding function
3. B computes and returns s' = S_B(m')
4. A sends m' to B for signature


### Why can we say that a blind signature allows A to obtain a signature from B on a message that B has never seen?

> Think back to what B actually receives: the message m or a transformed version of it?

1. [ ] Because B signs the message m directly but never reads it, simply computing its signature without analyzing it.
    > Incorrect: the key point is not that B doesn't read m, but that B never receives m in its original form.
1. [x] Because B only receives and signs the blinded version $m' = f(m)$, and it is only A, by applying the unblinding function g, who obtains the signature corresponding to the actual message m.
    > Correct: this is exactly the mechanism described in the course, exploiting the multiplicative property of RSA.
1. [ ] Because A sends the message m in the clear but encrypted with B's public key, which B therefore cannot decrypt.
    > Incorrect: the mechanism does not rely on encrypting the message but on the blinding/unblinding functions.
1. [ ] Because B entirely delegates the computation of the signature to A, who has access to B's private key.
    > Incorrect: B keeps its private key and performs the signature computation on m' itself.


### In the Rabin signature process, the signature s is computed as a square root of $m_R$ modulo n. What does the course specify about this?

> How many distinct square roots does a value have modulo a product of two large primes?

1. [ ] There is only one possible square root, which makes the computation deterministic.
    > Incorrect: the course states that there are 4 possible square roots.
1. [x] There are 4 possible square roots modulo n, and A sends only one of them as the signature s.
    > Correct: this is exactly what the course states about the Rabin signature.
1. [ ] The number of square roots depends on the size of the message and not on n.
    > Incorrect: this number follows from the structure of n = pq, not from the message size.
1. [ ] A must send all 4 square roots to B for verification to work.
    > Incorrect: only one of the 4 roots is sent as the signature.

> Compare what each algorithm uses to perform the signing operation (exponentiation vs. square root).

1. [ ] RSA's private key is (p,q), while Rabin's is the exponent d.
    > Incorrect: it's the opposite: RSA uses the exponent d as the private key, Rabin uses (p,q) directly.
1. [x] RSA's private key is the signature exponent d, while Rabin's private key is directly the pair of prime factors (p,q), used to compute modular square roots.
    > Correct: this is the distinction made in the "Key Generation" sections for RSA and Rabin.
1. [ ] RSA and Rabin use exactly the same private key, only the signature formula differs.
    > Incorrect: the private keys themselves differ, not just the formula applied.
1. [ ] Rabin's private key includes a generator α, unlike RSA's.
    > Incorrect: the generator α appears in the ElGamal scheme, not in Rabin.


### On which mathematical problem does the security of the ElGamal signature process rely?

> Think about the nature of the number a, of α, and of y = α^a mod p.

1. [ ] The problem of factoring large numbers (as in RSA).
    > Incorrect: this problem corresponds to RSA and Rabin, not ElGamal.
1. [x] The discrete logarithm problem (DLP).
    > Correct: the course explicitly associates ElGamal with the discrete logarithm problem, notably in the summary table.
1. [ ] The modular square root problem (SQROOTP).
    > Incorrect: this problem corresponds to the Rabin process.
1. [ ] No particular mathematical problem is required, security comes solely from the length of p.
    > Incorrect: the length of p alone is not enough, the hardness of DLP is essential.

1. [x] Because computing the signature requires $k^{-1} \bmod (p-1)$, which only exists if k and (p-1) are coprime.
    > Correct: without this condition, the modular inverse of k used to compute s could not be computed.
1. [ ] Because this condition guarantees that the private key a remains secret.
    > Incorrect: the secrecy of a relies on the hardness of the discrete logarithm, not on this condition on k.
1. [ ] Because it speeds up the computation of α^k mod p.

> Go back to the formula for computing s, which combines k, m_h, a and r.

- [x] r is computed from a random number k, independently of the message: $r = \alpha^k \bmod p$.
    > Correct: r depends only on k and not on the message digest.
- [x] s combines the message digest $m_h$, the private key a, r, and the inverse of k modulo (p-1).
    > Correct: this is exactly the formula $s = k^{-1}(m_h - ar) \bmod (p-1)$ given in the course.
- [ ] r and s are both independent of the message m.
    > Incorrect: s explicitly depends on $m_h = H(m)$, unlike r.
- [ ] s is computed solely from A's public key, without using its private key.
    > Incorrect: computing s directly uses a, A's private key.

> Think back to which variant of the scheme is mentioned as allowing recovery.

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False

### How is the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA), a NIST-approved standard, constructed according to the course?

> Think back to the explicit link made between DSA, ElGamal, and a particular hash function.

1. [ ] DSA is a completely independent algorithm from ElGamal, based on factorization.

1. [x] DSA is a direct derivative of the ElGamal scheme, using the SHA-1 hash function.

1. [ ] DSA replaces the public key with a symmetric key shared between signer and verifier.

1. [ ] DSA is identical to the RSA scheme, only the name changes.

1. [ ] It is derived from RSA and relies on the difficulty of factorization.

1. [x] It is derived from the ElGamal signature scheme, applied on elliptic curves, and its security relies on ECDLP.
    > Correct: this is exactly what the course states about the use of ECDSA by Bitcoin and Ethereum.
1. [ ] It is derived from Rabin and relies on computing modular square roots on elliptic curves.

1. [ ] It does not rely on any hard mathematical problem, its security comes solely from the secrecy of the protocol.
    > Incorrect: its security explicitly relies on the hardness of ECDLP.


### According to the course's summary table, which statements are correct?

> Think back to the "Message Recovery" column and the "Underlying Problem" column for each scheme listed.

- [x] RSA and Chaum's scheme (blind signatures) share the same underlying problem, RSAP.
    > Correct: the table associates RSAP with both RSA (classic signatures) and Chaum (blind signatures).
- [x] ElGamal and DSS do not allow message recovery and both rely on DLP.
    > Correct: the table shows "no" for Message Recovery and "DLP" for both schemes.
- [ ] One-time schemes like Lamport systematically rely on the discrete logarithm problem.
    > Incorrect: the table states that their security depends on the one-way function (OWF) used, not specifically on DLP.
- [ ] Rabin does not allow message recovery, unlike RSA.
    > Incorrect: the table shows "yes" for Message Recovery for both Rabin and RSA.

> Think back to who chooses the message involved in the forgery: the adversary or not.

1. [ ] There is no difference, these are two names for the same breaking criterion.
    > Incorrect: the course clearly distinguishes these two criteria among the ways to "break" a scheme.
1. [x] In selective forgery, the adversary manages to forge a valid signature for a message fixed in advance, whereas in existential forgery, the adversary only manages to forge a signature for at least one message, without controlling it.
    > Correct: this is exactly the distinction given in the course between these two success criteria for the adversary.
1. [ ] Selective forgery requires computing the signer's private key, unlike existential forgery.

1. [ ] Existential forgery is strictly harder to achieve than selective forgery.

- [x] Known-messages attack

- [x] Chosen-messages attack
    > Correct: this attack assumes the adversary was able to choose messages and obtain their signatures.
- [x] Adaptive chosen-messages attack
    > Correct: this attack goes further by allowing the adversary to choose its messages adaptively, based on signatures already obtained.
- [ ] Key-only attack
    > Incorrect: this attack assumes, on the contrary, that the adversary knows only the signer's public key, without access to signatures.

> Combine the type of access the adversary has with the severity level of the break achieved.

1. [ ] A chosen-messages attack resulting in an existential forgery.
    > Incorrect: the adversary used only the public key, not signatures obtained on chosen messages.
1. [x] A key-only attack resulting in a total break, the most severe breaking criterion for a digital signature scheme.
    > Correct: the adversary had access only to the public key (key-only attack) and succeeded in computing the private key, which corresponds to a total break.
1. [ ] An adaptive chosen-messages attack resulting in a selective forgery.
    > Incorrect: no signature of a chosen message was used in this scenario, only the public key.
1. [ ] No criterion from the course matches this situation, since computing the private key is not considered breaking the scheme.
    > Incorrect: computing the private key is precisely the example given in the course for the total break criterion.

- [ ] r and s are both independent of the message m.
    > Incorrect: s explicitly depends on $m_h = H(m)$, unlike r.
- [ ] s is computed solely from A's public key, without using its private key.
    > Incorrect: computing s directly uses a, A's private key.


### The ElGamal scheme, as presented in the course, natively allows message recovery from the signature.

> Think back to which variant of the scheme is mentioned as allowing recovery.

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: the course specifies that ElGamal, by construction, works only with appendix; it is the Nyberg-Rueppel scheme, a derived variant, that introduces message recovery.


### How is the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA), a NIST-approved standard, constructed according to the course?

> Think back to the explicit link made between DSA, ElGamal, and a particular hash function.

1. [ ] DSA is a completely independent algorithm from ElGamal, based on factorization.
    > Incorrect: the course states, on the contrary, that DSA is a direct derivative of the ElGamal scheme.
1. [x] DSA is a direct derivative of the ElGamal scheme, using the SHA-1 hash function.
    > Correct: this is exactly what the course states about the DSA standard.
1. [ ] DSA replaces the public key with a symmetric key shared between signer and verifier.
    > Incorrect: DSA remains a public-key scheme, like the ElGamal scheme it derives from.
1. [ ] DSA is identical to the RSA scheme, only the name changes.
    > Incorrect: DSA is associated with the discrete logarithm problem, not factorization as in RSA.


### Bitcoin and Ethereum use the ECDSA algorithm to authenticate their transactions. From which signature scheme is ECDSA derived, and on which problem does its security rely?

> Think back to the full name of ECDSA and what the acronym ECDLP means.

1. [ ] It is derived from RSA and relies on the difficulty of factorization.
    > Incorrect: ECDSA is not derived from RSA according to the course.
1. [x] It is derived from the ElGamal signature scheme, applied on elliptic curves, and its security relies on ECDLP.
    > Correct: this is exactly what the course states about the use of ECDSA by Bitcoin and Ethereum.
1. [ ] It is derived from Rabin and relies on computing modular square roots on elliptic curves.
    > Incorrect: ECDSA is presented as a derivative of ElGamal, not of Rabin.
1. [ ] It does not rely on any hard mathematical problem, its security comes solely from the secrecy of the protocol.
    > Incorrect: its security explicitly relies on the hardness of ECDLP.


### According to the course's summary table, which statements are correct?

> Think back to the "Message Recovery" column and the "Underlying Problem" column for each scheme listed.

- [x] RSA and Chaum's scheme (blind signatures) share the same underlying problem, RSAP.
    > Correct: the table associates RSAP with both RSA (classic signatures) and Chaum (blind signatures).
- [x] ElGamal and DSS do not allow message recovery and both rely on DLP.
    > Correct: the table shows "no" for Message Recovery and "DLP" for both schemes.
- [ ] One-time schemes like Lamport systematically rely on the discrete logarithm problem.
    > Incorrect: the table states that their security depends on the one-way function (OWF) used, not specifically on DLP.
- [ ] Rabin does not allow message recovery, unlike RSA.
    > Incorrect: the table shows "yes" for Message Recovery for both Rabin and RSA.


### What is the fundamental difference between selective forgery and existential forgery?

> Think back to who chooses the message involved in the forgery: the adversary or not.

1. [ ] There is no difference, these are two names for the same breaking criterion.
    > Incorrect: the course clearly distinguishes these two criteria among the ways to "break" a scheme.
1. [x] In selective forgery, the adversary manages to forge a valid signature for a message fixed in advance, whereas in existential forgery, the adversary only manages to forge a signature for at least one message, without controlling it.
    > Correct: this is exactly the distinction given in the course between these two success criteria for the adversary.
1. [ ] Selective forgery requires computing the signer's private key, unlike existential forgery.
    > Incorrect: computing the private key corresponds to the "total break" criterion, a third criterion distinct from the two forgeries.
1. [ ] Existential forgery is strictly harder to achieve than selective forgery.
    > Incorrect: the opposite is generally true: controlling the message makes the attack more constrained, so selective forgery is more demanding for the adversary.


### Among the following types of attacks against a digital signature scheme, which assume that the adversary has access to signatures corresponding to messages, and not solely to the signer's public key?

> Go back to the distinction made between "key-only" attacks and "message-based" attacks.

- [x] Known-messages attack
    > Correct: this attack assumes the adversary has signatures of known messages.
- [x] Chosen-messages attack
    > Correct: this attack assumes the adversary was able to choose messages and obtain their signatures.
- [x] Adaptive chosen-messages attack
    > Correct: this attack goes further by allowing the adversary to choose its messages adaptively, based on signatures already obtained.
- [ ] Key-only attack
    > Incorrect: this attack assumes, on the contrary, that the adversary knows only the signer's public key, without access to signatures.


### An adversary knowing only the signer's public key nevertheless manages to compute its private key. What type of attack did it carry out, and what success criterion did it achieve?

> Combine the type of access the adversary has with the severity level of the break achieved.

1. [ ] A chosen-messages attack resulting in an existential forgery.
    > Incorrect: the adversary used only the public key, not signatures obtained on chosen messages.
1. [x] A key-only attack resulting in a total break, the most severe breaking criterion for a digital signature scheme.
    > Correct: the adversary had access only to the public key (key-only attack) and succeeded in computing the private key, which corresponds to a total break.
1. [ ] An adaptive chosen-messages attack resulting in a selective forgery.
    > Incorrect: no signature of a chosen message was used in this scenario, only the public key.
1. [ ] No criterion from the course matches this situation, since computing the private key is not considered breaking the scheme.
    > Incorrect: computing the private key is precisely the example given in the course for the total break criterion.

title: Information System Security
text:
This quiz covers the entire chapter: one-way functions, definitions and properties of hash functions, MDCs and MACs, the birthday paradox, constructions based on encryption systems, customized functions (MD5, SHA), CBC-MAC, NMAC/HMAC, and applications (integrity, blockchain, salted passwords).



### Which property necessarily characterizes any hash function, whether keyed or not?

> Think back to the two properties listed in the general definition of a hash function, even before the question of the key.

1. [ ] Collision resistance
1. [x] Compression and ease of computation
    > Correct: these are the two fundamental properties required of any hash function, regardless of its category.
1. [ ] Computation-resistance
1. [ ] The mandatory use of a secret key





### A one-way function (OWF) is defined as a function for which...

> Think about the asymmetry between the forward direction and the reverse direction of the computation.

1. [ ] it is impossible to compute f(x) for any x
1. [x] f(x) is easy to compute, but recovering x from y = f(x) is computationally infeasible for the vast majority of y
    > Correct: this is exactly the computational asymmetry that defines an OWF.
1. [ ] f is bijective and therefore always invertible with additional computation
1. [ ] f necessarily requires a secret key to be computed





### Why does the function f(x) = E_k(x) alone (without XOR with x) not constitute a valid one-way function?

> Ask yourself what happens if the key k used by the encryption system E is known.

1. [ ] Because E_k(x) is always too slow to compute
1. [x] Because E, like DES, is reversible as soon as the key k is known
    > Correct: unlike E_k(x) XOR x, a classical block cipher remains reversible with the key, which cancels the one-way character.
1. [ ] Because E_k(x) always produces an output of variable size
1. [ ] Because the XOR is essential for compression





### An MDC (manipulation detection code) is distinguished from a MAC mainly by the fact that...

> Focus on the presence or absence of a shared secret in the computation.

- [x] an MDC is a function without a key (unkeyed)
    > Correct: an MDC does not involve any secret key in its computation.
- [ ] an MDC allows the source of a message to be authenticated without an additional mechanism
    > Incorrect: this is precisely what a MAC allows, not an MDC alone.
- [x] an MDC requires an additional mechanism (signature, secure channel, encryption) to guarantee the authenticity of the source
    > Correct: on its own, an MDC only provides an integrity service, not source authentication.
- [ ] an MDC always uses a 512-bit key
    > Incorrect: this key size concerns the HMAC construction, not MDCs in general.





### Among the following statements about the three basic properties of hash functions, which are correct?

> Reread carefully the difference between "given y, find x" and "given x and its image, find a different x'".

- [x] Preimage resistance concerns the difficulty of recovering x from y = h(x)
    > Correct: this is the exact definition of preimage resistance.
- [ ] 2nd-preimage resistance only applies to keyed functions
    > Incorrect: it applies to MDCs, which are unkeyed functions.
- [x] Collision resistance implies 2nd-preimage resistance
    > Correct: the course states that property 3 implies property 2.
- [ ] Preimage resistance is always weaker to break than collision resistance
    > Incorrect: it's the opposite: breaking collision resistance generally requires fewer trials (2^(n/2)) than breaking preimage resistance (2^n).





### The function f(x) = x² mod n (with n = pq unknown) is an OWF but not an OWHF. Why?

> Look for a trivial and obvious collision on this function, independent of the difficulty of factoring n.

1. [ ] Because it is not easy to compute
1. [ ] Because it does not compress the input
1. [x] Because for any x, -x constitutes a trivial collision: h(x) = h(-x)
    > Correct: this obvious collision violates the 2nd-preimage resistance required of an OWHF, even though inversion remains hard.
1. [ ] Because it requires knowledge of p and q to be computed





### Does the fact that a key k cannot be recovered from known pairs (x_i, h_k(x_i)) (key non-recovery) automatically imply the computation-resistance of a MAC?

> Think about chosen/known-plaintext attacks that could produce a forged pair without ever revealing the key.

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: the course explicitly states that key non-recovery does not imply computation-resistance, because chosen/known-plaintext attacks can allow forging a pair (x, h_k(x)) without ever recovering k.





### A student controls an original text that they have signed by an authority, then wants to apply that same signature to a forged text of their choice. Which type of attack must they succeed at?

> They choose both texts themselves: which resistance property does this correspond to?

1. [ ] Preimage resistance
1. [ ] 2nd-preimage resistance
1. [x] Collision resistance
    > Correct: since the attacker controls both messages, they are looking for a pair of distinct preimages having the same digest — this is collision search.
1. [ ] Key non-recovery





### An attacker has an original text they do not control, along with its associated signature. They want to create a forged text carrying the same signature. Which type of attack must they succeed at?

> This time, only one of the two texts is fixed: the one they do not control.

1. [ ] Preimage resistance
1. [x] 2nd-preimage resistance
    > Correct: the attacker starts from a fixed x (the imposed original text) and looks for a different x' producing the same digest — this is exactly the definition of 2nd-preimage resistance.
1. [ ] Collision resistance
1. [ ] Key non-recovery





### For an m-bit digest, what is approximately the number of trials needed to find, with a probability of 0.5, a value y such that h(x) = h(y) for a fixed x?

> Go back to the calculation k = n/2 obtained in the course, with n = 2^m possible outputs.

1. [ ] 2^m
1. [x] 2^(m-1)
    > Correct: the course establishes that k = n/2 = 2^m/2 = 2^(m-1) trials suffice for a probability of 0.5 of finding a y such that h(x) = h(y).
1. [ ] 2^(m/2)
1. [ ] m/2





### According to the birthday paradox applied to hash functions with 2^m possible outputs, how many inputs must be tested to obtain a collision with a probability greater than 0.5?

> This number is significantly smaller than that needed to find a preimage: it is the square root of the number of outputs.

1. [ ] 2^m
1. [ ] 2^(m-1)
1. [x] 2^(m/2)
    > Correct: the birthday paradox shows that k = 2^(m/2) trials suffice to exceed a probability of 0.5 of obtaining a collision.
1. [ ] m/2





### According to the course's summary table, what minimum digest size is recommended for a collision-resistant function (CRHF) to offer effective security of at least 80 bits?

> The cost of a collision attack is on the order of 2^(n/2): what digest size n then gives a security of 2^80?

1. [ ] 80 bits
1. [ ] 128 bits
1. [x] 160 bits
    > Correct: since a collision attack costs 2^(n/2), n ≥ 160 bits is needed to obtain effective security of 2^80, in line with the course table.
1. [ ] 256 bits





### Why does the 64-bit "nominal width" of encryption systems like DES pose a problem for directly building a CRHF?

> Relate this width to the minimum recommended digest size for collision resistance.

1. [ ] Because 64 bits is a block size too large to be processed efficiently
1. [x] Because 64 bits is insufficient compared to the recommended digest size (at least 160 bits) needed to resist collision attacks
    > Correct: the course explicitly states that the 64-bit nominal width of DES is not enough to build CRHFs, hence the need to combine several encryption boxes (MDC-2, MDC-4).
1. [ ] Because DES can only process messages of 64 bits in total
1. [ ] Because 64 bits makes the encryption reversible





### MDC-2 and MDC-4 work around the width limitation of DES boxes by...

> Think about the principle mentioned in the course for obtaining digests longer than the nominal width of a single encryption box.

1. [ ] reducing the size of the DES key
1. [x] respectively combining 2 and 4 DES boxes to obtain a 128-bit digest
    > Correct: the course states that MDC-2 and MDC-4 respectively use 2 and 4 DES boxes to produce a 128-bit digest in total.
1. [ ] removing the chaining operations between blocks
1. [ ] applying a single DES box directly to 128-bit text blocks





### What makes the construction process of MDCs based on encryption systems irreversible, when the underlying encryption system (e.g. DES) is reversible?

> The course mentions two mechanisms combined around successive blocks.

1. [ ] The mere fact of using 64-bit blocks
1. [x] The chaining operations between successive blocks combined with logical functions such as XOR
    > Correct: the course states that compression relies on chaining operations and logical functions (fundamentally XOR), which makes the whole process irreversible despite the reversibility of the encryption box alone.
1. [ ] The systematic use of a 512-bit secret key
1. [ ] The complete removal of the input text blocks





### The same generic scheme (chaining a compression function with previous blocks) gives rise to several constructions depending on how the previous input, the message, and the key are combined. Which constructions correspond to this principle according to the course?

> These are the three generic models presented in the course for encryption-based MDCs.

- [x] Matyas-Meyer-Oseas
    > Correct: this is one of the three generic models cited in the course.
- [x] Davies-Meyer
    > Correct: this is also one of the three generic models cited in the course.
- [x] Miyaguchi-Preneel
    > Correct: this is the third generic model cited in the course.
- [ ] HMAC
    > Incorrect: HMAC is not a generic model of encryption-based MDC, but a Nested MAC built from an unkeyed hash function such as SHA-1 or SHA-256.





### In December 2008, researchers exploited controlled collisions on MD5 to...

> Think back to the concrete and alarming application mentioned for this attack.

1. [ ] break DES in polynomial time
1. [x] create a rogue Certification Authority allowing certificates to be forged that are accepted by any browser
    > Correct: this is exactly the result obtained, illustrating that a controlled (rather than merely arbitrary) collision can have serious practical consequences.
1. [ ] recover the secret key used by an HMAC
1. [ ] demonstrate that SHA-3 was vulnerable





### Why are the attacks found by X. Wang et al. against MD5 and SHA-1 considered particularly significant, beyond simply finding collisions?

> Compare the number of operations they require to the number theoretically expected for the collision resistance of these functions.

1. [ ] Because they require more operations than predicted by theory
1. [x] Because they reduce the number of operations needed to well below the theoretical bound of 2^(n/2), thanks to analytical approaches rather than brute force
    > Correct: for example, collisions on SHA-1 were found in 2^63 operations instead of the theoretically expected 2^80, via an analytical approach rather than simple brute force.
1. [ ] Because they only target preimage resistance, never collision resistance
1. [ ] Because they only apply to keyed functions such as HMACs





### A Nested MAC (NMAC), composed of two families of functions G and H, offers a security that depends on two conditions. Which ones?

> Reread the definition that distinguishes the role of the outer function G from that of the inner function H.

- [x] G must be collision resistant
    > Correct: this is the first security condition stated in the course for an NMAC.
- [ ] G must be a keyless function
    > Incorrect: in an NMAC, G is a family of functions parameterized by a key, just like H.
- [x] H must resist attacks specific to MACs (impossibility of forging a valid pair (x,y) without knowing the key)
    > Correct: this is the second condition stated in the course.
- [ ] H must produce a digest of at least 512 bits
    > Incorrect: this size corresponds to the ipad/opad constants and the key used by HMAC, not a general requirement on H in an NMAC.





### How does an HMAC differ structurally from a MAC such as CBC-MAC?

> Compare the nature of the base function used by each of these two mechanisms.

1. [ ] CBC-MAC uses SHA-256 while HMAC uses DES
1. [x] HMAC is a Nested MAC built from an unkeyed hash function (such as SHA-1 or SHA-256), whereas CBC-MAC is built directly from a symmetric block cipher (DES)
    > Correct: this is precisely the distinction established in the course between these two approaches to building a MAC.
1. [ ] CBC-MAC uses two distinct keys k and l, whereas HMAC uses none
1. [ ] HMAC can only produce a 64-bit digest, like CBC-MAC





### Why are known attacks against functions of the SHA family harder to carry out when these functions are used within an HMAC?

> Compare what an attacker knows in a direct attack on SHA-1 versus an attack on HMAC-SHA1.

1. [ ] Because HMAC produces a digest twice as long as SHA alone
1. [x] Because the presence of the secret key k in the HMAC computation prevents the attacker from freely reproducing the conditions exploited by analytical attacks on the bare hash function
    > Correct: the course points out that the involvement of key k in HMAC makes known attacks on the SHA family harder to carry out.
1. [ ] Because HMAC never actually uses the SHA function internally
1. [ ] Because HMAC completely eliminates the compression operation





### The historical UNIX password storage system had a weakness exploitable by an off-line dictionary attack. What was the main cause of this weakness before the introduction of the salt?

> Think about what happens when two different users choose the same password, with a deterministic hash function.

1. [ ] The hash function used was not collision resistant
1. [x] Since the hash function was deterministic, the same password always produced the same result, making it possible to precompute a "codebook" associating common passwords with digests
    > Correct: this is exactly the problem identified in the course, solved by adding a random element (the salt).
1. [ ] The password file was not accessible to anyone
1. [ ] The digest size used was 512 bits, which made it too predictable





### Adding a 12-bit salt to each UNIX password before computing the hash function introduces a random factor of how many possibilities per password?

> How many combinations does 12 bits correspond to? Use 2 to the power of 12.

1. [ ] 12
1. [ ] 144
1. [x] 4096
    > Correct: 2^12 = 4096, which exactly matches the value given in the course for the random factor introduced by the salt.
1. [ ] 65536





### Does the UNIX salt prevent an attacker from guessing the password of a particular user if they already know that user's salt?

> Distinguish clearly between the goal of the salt (preventing global precomputation and duplicate detection) and the individual protection of a given password.

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: the salt mainly prevents the reuse of a single precomputed "codebook" against all users and prevents the detection of identical passwords between users; a targeted attack on a user whose salt is known remains possible by recomputing the hash for each candidate with that specific salt.





### In the one-time password (S-Key) authentication mechanism, starting from a secret seed x0, a chain is built: x1 = h(x0), x2 = h(x1), ..., xn = h(x(n-1)). Why does this construction allow secure authentication even if an attacker intercepts the value transmitted at each login?

> Think about the direction in which the user traverses the chain across successive logins, and the difficulty of inverting a hash function.

1. [ ] Because each transmitted value is encrypted with a different key
1. [x] Because the user transmits the chain in reverse order of its construction (from xn towards x0), and recovering x(n-1) from an intercepted xn would require inverting the hash function, which is computationally infeasible
    > Correct: the security of the S-Key system relies on the preimage resistance of h: knowing x_n does not allow computing x_(n-1), which will nevertheless be the value required at the next login.
1. [ ] Because the hash chain changes function h at each step
1. [ ] Because the system never stores any value from the chain





### In the context of blockchain mining (proof of work), the difficulty of the cryptographic puzzle concretely corresponds to...

> Relate this difficulty to one of the three resistance properties studied in this chapter, applied to a portion of the digest's bits.

1. [ ] finding the secret key used by the block's hash function
1. [x] finding a pseudo-collision, i.e. a digest whose most significant bits are below a given target, by varying the nonce
    > Correct: the course states that mining consists of finding pseudo-collisions in the hash function, with the target defining the number of most significant bits involved.
1. [ ] breaking the 2nd-preimage resistance of an already published transaction
1. [ ] decrypting previous transactions on the blockchain





### Why is falsifying data already recorded in a blockchain considered practically impossible?

> Think about what the chaining of blocks by hash functions implies, combined with the computing power already invested by all the honest miners.

1. [ ] Because the blockchain is encrypted with a secret key known only to the miners
1. [x] Because modifying a block would require redoing the mining work (proof of work) for that block and all subsequent ones, with a computational effort greater than that of all honest miners combined
    > Correct: this is exactly the guarantee described in the course for the immutability of the public ledger that constitutes the blockchain.
1. [ ] Because each transaction is individually signed by a central authority
1. [ ] Because the digest size used makes any collision mathematically impossible





### Put the historical development of the main customized hash functions mentioned in the course in chronological order.

> Think about the historical evolution in response to successively discovered attacks.

1. MD5 (Rivest, 1992)
2. SHA-0 (NIST, 1993)
3. SHA-1 (NIST, 1995)
4. SHA-2 (NIST, FIPS 190-3)
5. SHA-3 / Keccak (chosen by NIST in 2012)





### Put the generic operating steps of a customized hash function (customized MDC) as described in the course in order.

> Think about what must be done even before starting to process the data blocks, then the order in which the rounds and chaining occur.

1. Initialization of the data via padding and appending the message length
2. Sequential application of the rounds to each block, combining logical operations and rotations with predefined constants
3. Chaining of the outputs of each round with the following blocks
4. Obtaining the final digest after processing all the blocks





### Put the password verification steps in the salted UNIX system described in the course in order.

> The salt must be available before anything can be recomputed.

1. The system retrieves the salt associated with the user, stored together with the digest
2. The user enters their password in cleartext
3. The system concatenates the salt and the entered password, then applies the hash function
4. The system compares the result obtained to the stored digest to grant or deny access
